head: environment
name: Exact asymptotic rate

title: Proof
body_md:
Set $s=\sqrt\kappa>1$.
For the lower bound, suppose $q_\star(s)>q_{\mathrm{quad}}(s)$.
An optimal angular pair can then be chosen with a finitely supported measure, so the construction in Section~\ref{sec:variational} uses finitely many planar trajectories.
We construct a function in $\mathcal F_{1,\kappa}$ for which Nesterov's method, initialized with $x_{-1}=x_0$, attains this asymptotic factor.
If $q_\star(s)=q_{\mathrm{quad}}(s)$, the quadratic $f(x)=x^2/2$ attains the factor.
For the upper bound, fix $q\in(q_\star(s),1)$.
The interpolation conditions are infeasible at this factor.
A separation argument gives a nonnegative combination of finitely many cyclic monotonicity inequalities.
After rescaling the iterates, we sum these inequalities and use the NAG recurrence to bound their squared norms.
The key identity averages a finite sum of integer powers over equally spaced points on the unit circle.
A finite induction first establishes that the sums of squared norms are finite, and then gives
\[
 \|x_t-x_\star\|^2\leq bq^t\|x_0-x_\star\|^2,
\]
where $b$ depends only on $s$ and $q$.
Taking $t$th roots and letting $t\to\infty$ gives $\rho_{\mathrm{hor}}(s^2)\leq q$.
Letting $q\downarrowq_\star(s)$ proves the upper bound.
The full proof is given in Appendix~\ref{app:generic-bridges}.

At $\kappa=(1421/1250)^2$, the exact factor $q_\star(1421/1250)$ has a minimal
polynomial of degree $20$ over $\mathbb Q$, with Galois group $S_{20}$.
Consequently, no formula built from rational functions of $s$ with rational
coefficients and finitely many radicals can be defined and valid for every
$s>1$. Appendix~\ref{app:rate-radicals} gives the polynomial and its exact
certificate. This does not exclude other notions of closed form.

The necessary condition $\bar c_{01}(\nu)\geq0$ gives an upper bound on the exact factor.
For the lower bound, fix $2/3<\alpha<3/4$.
For all sufficiently large $\kappa$, we construct a probability measure satisfying every interpolation inequality with $\varphi_0=0$ at
\[

\]
Letting $\alpha\downarrow2/3$ gives the matching coefficient $4/3$.

label: cor:metrics
title: Corollary
head: environment
name: Function gap and gradient norm

title: Proof
body_md:
For every $f\in\mathcal F_{1,\kappa}$ and $x$, strong convexity and smoothness give
\[
 \frac12\|x-x_\star\|^2\leq f(x)-f(x_\star)
 \leq\frac\kappa2\|x-x_\star\|^2,
 \qquad
 \|x-x_\star\|^2\leq\|\nabla f(x)\|^2
 \leq\kappa^2\|x-x_\star\|^2.
\]
Dividing by the corresponding initial values bounds the first ratio between $\kappa^{-1}R_t$ and $\kappa R_t$, and the second between $\kappa^{-2}R_t$ and $\kappa^2R_t$.
These constants depend only on $\kappa$, so the bounds remain valid when taking the supremum over dimensions, functions, and initial points.
Their $t$th roots tend to one, which proves equality of the asymptotic factors in both definitions.

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $s>1$, $q\in(0,1)$, and a probability measure $\nu$.
For integers $t,u\geq1$, define
\[
 b_t=\frac{\bar c_{0t}(\nu)}{1-q^t},
 \qquad a_u=-\frac{\bar c_{u0}(\nu)}{1-q^u}.
\]
The interpolation conditions ask for a scalar between every lower bound $a_u$ and every upper bound $b_t$.
Assume cyclic monotonicity and consider the finite cycle
\[
 0,t,2t,\ldots,ut,(t-1)u,(t-2)u,\ldots,u,0.
\]
It first takes $u$ steps of length $t$ upwards, then $t$ steps of length $u$ downwards.
Repeated indices are allowed.
Using $\bar c_{i+k,j+k}=q^k\bar c_{ij}$, its cost is
\[
 \bar c_{0t}\sum_{j=0}^{u-1}q^{jt}
 +\bar c_{u0}\sum_{j=0}^{t-1}q^{ju}
 =(1-q^{tu})(b_t-a_u)\geq0.
\]
Since $q<1$, this gives $a_u\leq b_t$ for every $t,u\geq1$.
Consequently,
\[
 \varphi_0:=\sup_{u\geq1}a_u
\]
is finite, lies above every $a_u$, and lies below every $b_t$.
This proves \eqref{eq:star-feasible}.

Conversely, suppose \eqref{eq:star-feasible} holds and set $\varphi_i=q^i\varphi_0$.
For $j>i$, apply the upper bound in \eqref{eq:star-feasible} with $t=j-i$ to obtain
\[
 \varphi_i-\varphi_j
 =q^i(1-q^{j-i})\varphi_0
 \leq q^i\bar c_{0,j-i}=\bar c_{ij}.
\]
For $i>j$, the lower bound in \eqref{eq:star-feasible} with $t=i-j$ gives the same inequality.
The case $i=j$ is immediate.
Summing these inequalities around any finite cycle proves cyclic monotonicity.

label: lem:closed-rate-problem
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Feasibility, the classical bound, and attainment

label: eq:star-origin-bounds
title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $(q,\nu,\varphi_0)$ satisfying \eqref{eq:star-feasible}.
Since $|z|=\sqrt q<1$, the edge formula gives the uniform limits
\[
 c_{t0}(\theta)\longrightarrow0,
 \qquad c_{0t}(\theta)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Re}d_s(z).
\]
Writing $m=\int\operatorname{Re}d_s(z)\,d\nu$, the interpolation conditions imply
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:star-origin-bounds}
 0\leq\varphi_0\leq m,
 \qquad \bar c_{01}(\nu)\geq(1-q)\varphi_0\geq0.
\end{equation}
These bounds also justify including the optimum, with $(\sigma,r,\varphi)=(0,0,0)$.
Indeed, for the prescribed trajectory they give
$0\leq\varphi_i=q^i\varphi_0\leq q^im=\langle r_i,\sigma_i\rangle$, precisely the two interpolation inequalities with the optimum.

We show directly that $q\geq1-1/s$ is impossible.
Put $a=1-1/s\in(0,1)$.
Expanding $c_{02}(\theta)$, which compares iterations $0$ and $2$, gives
\[
 \frac{c_{02}(\theta)}{s^2-1}
 =a^2-1+\frac{2a(1-q)}{\sqrt q}\cos\theta
       +\frac{q^2-a^2}{q}\cos(2\theta).
\]
If $q\geq a$, both cosine coefficients are nonnegative.
Since $\sqrt q\geq\sqrt a>a$, it follows that
\[
 c_{02}(\theta)\leq c_{02}(0)
 =-(s^2-1)(1-q)(1-a/\sqrt q)^2<0.
\]
This contradicts
$\bar c_{02}(\nu)\geq(1-q^2)\varphi_0\geq0$, which follows from
\eqref{eq:star-feasible} and \eqref{eq:star-origin-bounds}.
Thus every feasible factor satisfies $q<1-1/s$.

The choice $q=q_{\mathrm{quad}}(s)$ and $\nu=\delta_0$ has $d_s(z)=0$ and all cycle costs zero, so it is feasible with $\varphi_0=0$.
To prove attainment, restrict $q$ to the compact interval $[q_{\mathrm{quad}}(s),1-1/s]$ and impose all cycle inequalities on $(q,\nu)$.
For each fixed cycle its cost is jointly continuous in $q$ and $\theta$ on this interval times $[0,\pi]$.
Each averaged inequality therefore defines a closed set under convergence of $q$ and weak convergence of $\nu$.
Their intersection is a nonempty closed subset of the compact product
$[q_{\mathrm{quad}}(s),1-1/s]\times\mathcal P([0,\pi])$.
The continuous objective $q$ attains its maximum there.
Lemma~\ref{lem:stars} supplies the corresponding scalar $\varphi_0$.
Since smaller factors cannot improve on $q_{\mathrm{quad}}(s)$, this is the largest feasible factor.

label: lem:disk-radial-reweighting
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Radial reweighting

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $|z|^2\geq0$ and $\int |z|^2\,d\mu=m$, $\eta$ is a probability measure on $D_s$.
For every cycle $\gamma$, the shift identity \eqref{eq:disk-cost-shift} and feasibility of $\mu$ give
\[
 \int\mathcal C_\gamma^s\,d\eta
 =\frac1m\int |z|^2\mathcal C_\gamma^s\,d\mu
 =\frac1m\int\mathcal C_{\gamma+1}^s\,d\mu\geq0.
\]
Also $J(\eta)=\int |z|^4\,d\mu/m$, which proves the identity.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Probability measures on the compact disk form a weakly compact set.
Every cycle cost is continuous, so the feasible set of \eqref{eq:disk-rate-lp} is closed.
It is nonempty: $\delta_{\alpha_s}$ has zero costs and objective $\alpha_s^2=q_{\mathrm{quad}}(s)$.
Hence the feasible set is nonempty and compact under weak convergence.
Since $z\mapsto|z|^2$ is continuous and bounded on $D_s$, the objective $J$ is continuous under weak convergence.
The extreme value theorem, applied in this topology, therefore gives a maximum $m\geq q_{\mathrm{quad}}(s)>0$.
If an optimal measure $\mu$ had $\operatorname{Var}_\mu(|z|^2)>0$, Lemma~\ref{lem:disk-radial-reweighting} would give a feasible measure with a strictly larger objective value.
Thus every optimal measure $\mu$ satisfies $\operatorname{Var}_\mu(|z|^2)=0$ and is supported on the circle $|z|^2=m$, with $0<m\leq\alpha_s<1$.

We now prove the fixed-factor equivalence. For any $q\in\mathcal Q(s)$,
Lemma~\ref{lem:closed-rate-problem} gives $q\leq\alpha_s$.
Choose an angular measure $\nu$ satisfying \eqref{eq:star-feasible}.
Replace each angle $\theta$ by the point $\sqrt q\,e^{i\theta}$ to obtain a probability measure $\mu$ on the corresponding circle in $D_s$.
By Lemma~\ref{lem:stars}, $\nu$ satisfies all cycle inequalities.
The positive scaling in \eqref{eq:disk-cycle-cost} then makes $\mu$ feasible for \eqref{eq:disk-rate-lp}, with objective value $q$.
Conversely, let $\mu$ be feasible for \eqref{eq:disk-rate-lp} and supported on $|z|^2=q$ for some $q\in(0,1)$.
Map each point $z=\sqrt q\,e^{\pm i\theta}$ to $\theta\in[0,\pi]$ to obtain an angular probability measure $\nu$.
Conjugation preserves every cost, and division by the common positive factor $q^2/(s^2-1)$ gives all cycle inequalities for $\nu$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:stars} then gives a scalar $\varphi_0$ satisfying \eqref{eq:star-feasible}, so $q\in\mathcal Q(s)$.
This argument remains valid at $q=q_{\mathrm{quad}}(s)$, even where $d_s(z)=0$, because it does not divide by $d_s(z)$.

Applying this equivalence to an optimizing disk measure gives
$m\in\mathcal Q(s)$.
Conversely, for every $q\in\mathcal Q(s)$, the construction above gives a feasible measure for \eqref{eq:disk-rate-lp} with objective value $q$, so $q\leq m$.
Thus $m=\max\mathcal Q(s)$, proving \eqref{eq:qcyc}.
The lower bound follows from $q_{\mathrm{quad}}(s)\in\mathcal Q(s)$, and the upper bound
from Lemma~\ref{lem:closed-rate-problem}.

label: prop:disk-finite-dual
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Finite-index bounds and duality

title: Proof
body_md:
Each finite-index feasible set is closed in the compact probability space
and contains $\delta_{\alpha_s}$, so its maximum exists. The sets are
nested. A weak limit of optimizers along $n\to\infty$ satisfies every fixed
cycle constraint, since that constraint holds eventually. Continuity of
$J$ proves that the decreasing limit of $q_{\mathrm{rel},n}(s)$ equals $q_\star(s)$.

Integrating any polynomial inequality in \eqref{eq:disk-polynomial-dual}
against a feasible measure gives $J(\mu)\leq b$. Conversely, fix
$b>q_\star(s)$. Compactness supplies finitely many cycle constraints whose
intersection with $J(\mu)\geq b$ is already empty. Their compact convex
moment image is disjoint from
$\{t\in\mathbf R:t\geq b\}\times\mathbf R_+^{|\Gamma_0|}$.
Strict separation gives nonnegative coefficients
$(\lambda_0,(\eta_\gamma)_{\gamma\in\Gamma_0})$ with
\[
 \lambda_0|z|^2+\sum_{\gamma\in\Gamma_0}\eta_\gamma
           \mathcal C_\gamma^s(z)<\lambda_0b,
 \quad z\in D_s.
\]
The coefficient $\lambda_0$ is positive: otherwise evaluating at
$z=\alpha_s$, where all cycle costs vanish, contradicts strictness.
Division by $\lambda_0$ proves the claim.

label: lem:strict-alternative
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:strict-alternative}
Fix $s>1$ and $q\in(q_{\mathrm{quad}}(s),1)$.
For a finite cycle $\gamma=(i_0,i_1,\ldots,i_m=i_0)$, define the sum of the interpolation terms \eqref{eq:edge-cost} by
\[
 c_\gamma(\theta)=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}c_{i_j i_{j+1}}(\theta).
\]
Exactly one of the following holds:
\begin{enumerate}
 \item Every finite list of cycles $\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_n$ admits angles $\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_m\in[0,\pi]$ and weights $a_i\geq0$, with $1\leq m\leq n+1$, satisfying
 \[
  \sum_{i=1}^m a_i=1,
  \qquad
  \sum_{i=1}^m a_i c_{\gamma_j}(\theta_i)\geq0,
  \qquad j=1,\ldots,n.
 \]
 \item There are finitely many cycles $\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_n$
 and weights $w_j\geq0$ such that
 \[
  \sum_{j=1}^nw_j
  c_{\gamma_j}(\theta)<0,
  \qquad 0\leq\theta\leq\pi.
 \]
\end{enumerate}
The angles and weights in alternative~1 may depend on the selected cycles.
head: environment
name: Finite certificate of infeasibility

title: Proof
body_md:
For any fixed list $\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_n$, consider the cost vectors
\[
 (c_{\gamma_1}(\theta),\ldots,c_{\gamma_n}(\theta)),
 \qquad \theta\in[0,\pi].
\]
Their convex hull is compact because the cycle costs are continuous.
By Carath\'eodory's theorem, every point in this hull is a convex combination of at most $n+1$ cost vectors.
Thus the hull intersects $\mathbf R_+^n$ exactly when the inequalities in alternative~1 hold for the selected cycles.

If alternative~1 fails, choose a list for which the hull and $\mathbf R_+^n$ are disjoint.
The separating hyperplane theorem gives a vector $w$ such that
\[
 \max_{\theta\in[0,\pi]}\sum_{j=1}^n w_jc_{\gamma_j}(\theta)
 <\inf_{v\in\mathbf R_+^n}w^Tv.
\]
The vector $w$ must be nonnegative, since a negative component would make the infimum $-\infty$.
The infimum is therefore zero, which gives alternative~2.

If both alternatives held, choose angles and weights from alternative~1 for the cycles in alternative~2.
Then
\[
 0\leq\sum_{j=1}^n w_j\sum_{i=1}^m a_i c_{\gamma_j}(\theta_i)
 =\sum_{i=1}^m a_i\sum_{j=1}^n w_j c_{\gamma_j}(\theta_i)<0,
\]
a contradiction.
head: environment

label: lem:finite-optimal-support
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Finite support at the optimal factor

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $q_\star=q_\star(s)$ and choose an optimal pair $(\nu_\star,\varphi_0^\star)$.
We construct a function that vanishes on the support of $\nu_\star$ and has only finitely many zeros.
Since $q$ varies in this proof, we write $c_{ij}(q,\theta)$ for the term in \eqref{eq:edge-cost}, evaluated at $z=\sqrt q\,e^{i\theta}$ with $s$ fixed.
For $t\geq1$, put
\[
 u_t(q,\theta)=\frac{c_{0t}(q,\theta)}{1-q^t},
 \qquad v_t(q,\theta)=\frac{c_{t0}(q,\theta)}{1-q^t},
 \qquad d(q,\theta)=\operatorname{Re}d_s(\sqrt q\,e^{i\theta}).
\]
Here $u_t$ and $v_t$ compare iterations $0$ and $t$ in the two possible orders.
At $q_\star$, the interpolation inequalities give
$\int u_t\,d\nu_\star\geq\varphi_0^\star$ and
$\int v_t\,d\nu_\star\geq-\varphi_0^\star$.

Choose $q_\star<q_+<1$ and $q_n\downarrow q_\star$ with $q_\star<q_n\leq q_+$.
By Lemma~\ref{lem:strict-alternative} and the compactness argument above, there is a strict cycle separator at every $q_n$.
The interpolation term $c_{ij}(q,\theta)$ in \eqref{eq:edge-cost} compares iterations $i$ and $j$ and satisfies
\[
 c_{ij}(q,\theta)=
 \begin{cases}
  (q^i-q^j)u_{j-i}(q,\theta), & i<j,\\
  (q^j-q^i)v_{i-j}(q,\theta), & i>j,\\
  0, & i=j.
 \end{cases}
\]
For a cycle $\gamma=(i_0,\ldots,i_m=i_0)$, the differences telescope to $\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}(q^{i_k}-q^{i_{k+1}})=q^{i_0}-q^{i_m}=0$.
Since $0<q<1$, the positive differences are the coefficients of the $u_t$ terms, and the absolute values of the negative differences are the coefficients of the $v_t$ terms.
Their totals therefore agree for each cycle, and hence for every nonnegative weighted sum of cycles.
For each $n$, choose one strict separator at $q_n$ and expand its cycle costs using the displayed formula for $c_{ij}$.
Collect the coefficients of each $u_t(q_n,\theta)$ and $v_t(q_n,\theta)$.
Their common total is positive, since a zero total would make the separator identically zero.
Define $a_{t,n}$ and $b_{t,n}$ as these respective coefficients divided by their common total.
They are nonnegative, only finitely many are nonzero for each $n$, and
\[
 \sum_{t\geq1}a_{t,n}=\sum_{t\geq1}b_{t,n}=1.
\]
These coefficients depend on the separator chosen at $q_n$ and remain fixed as $q$ varies.
For $q\in[q_\star,q_+]$ and $\theta\in[0,\pi]$, define
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:lag-separator-limit}
 w_n(q,\theta)
 =\sum_{t\geq1}a_{t,n}u_t(q,\theta)
 +\sum_{t\geq1}b_{t,n}v_t(q,\theta).
\end{equation}
At $q=q_n$, this is the chosen separator divided by its positive normalizing constant, so $w_n(q_n,\theta)<0$ on $[0,\pi]$.
At $q=q_\star$, the interpolation inequalities and the two coefficient sums give $\int w_n(q_\star,\theta)\,d\nu_\star\geq\varphi_0^\star-\varphi_0^\star=0$.
Since $\sum_t a_{t,n}=1$, we can also write
\[
 w_n(q,\theta)=d(q,\theta)
 +\sum_{t\geq1}a_{t,n}\bigl(u_t(q,\theta)-d(q,\theta)\bigr)
 +\sum_{t\geq1}b_{t,n}v_t(q,\theta).
\]

We next bound $u_t-d$ and $v_t$ to justify taking a limit in $w_n$.
We also bound their derivatives with respect to $\theta$ to control the Taylor remainder of the limiting function later in the proof.
Throughout this calculation, $q$ is held fixed when differentiating.
With $z=\sqrt q\,e^{i\theta}$, the definitions and \eqref{eq:edge-cost} give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 u_t(q,\theta)-d(q,\theta)
 &=\frac{q^t d(q,\theta)-\operatorname{Re}[\overline{d_s(z)}\bar z^t]}{1-q^t},\\
 v_t(q,\theta)
 &=\frac{q^t d(q,\theta)-\operatorname{Re}[\overline{d_s(z)}z^t]}{1-q^t}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
To identify the cosine terms in these expressions, write \eqref{eq:nag-transfer} as
\[
 d_s(z)=-(s^2-1)\left(1-\frac{2(1-1/s)}{z}
 +\frac{(1-1/s)^2}{z^2}\right).
\]
Since $\operatorname{Re}(e^{ik\theta})=\cos(k\theta)$ and $\cos(-k\theta)=\cos(k\theta)$, both $u_t-d$ and $v_t$ are finite sums of $\cos(k\theta)$ with integer indices $0\leq k\leq t+2$.
For any finite sum $h(\theta)=\sum_k p_k\cos(k\theta)$, the triangle inequality gives $|h(\theta)|\leq\sum_k|p_k|$ at every angle.
The combined sum of the absolute values of the cosine coefficients of $u_t-d$ and $v_t$ is at most
\[
 \frac{2(s^2-1)(q^t+q^{t/2})}{1-q^t}
 \left(1+\frac{1-1/s}{\sqrt q}\right)^2
 \leq c r_+^t,
 \qquad q\in[q_\star,q_+],
\]
where
\[
 r_+=\sqrt{q_+}<1,\qquad
 c=\frac{4(s^2-1)}{1-q_+}
 \left(1+\frac{1-1/s}{\sqrt{q_\star}}\right)^2.
\]
Each differentiation multiplies the absolute value of a sine or cosine term's coefficient by its index $k$.
After $j$ derivatives, the absolute value of each coefficient is therefore multiplied by at most $(t+2)^j$.
Applying the same triangle inequality gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:lag-geometric-tails}
 \left|\frac{d^j}{d\theta^j}(u_t-d)\right|
 +\left|\frac{d^j}{d\theta^j}v_t\right|
 \leq c r_+^t(t+2)^j,
 \qquad j\geq0,\quad\theta\in\mathbf R.
\end{equation}
For $j=0$, this bounds the functions themselves and shows that $u_t-d$ and $v_t$ tend to zero uniformly in $q$ and $\theta$ on $[q_\star,q_+]\times[0,\pi]$.
The function $d$ is a linear combination of $1$, $\cos\theta$, and $\cos(2\theta)$, and satisfies $|\frac{d^j}{d\theta^j}d|\leq c2^j$.

The separator coefficients $a_{t,n}$ and $b_{t,n}$ lie in $[0,1]$.
Choose nested subsequences along which the coefficients converge for $t=1$, then for $t=2$, and so on.
Taking the $n$th element of the $n$th subsequence gives a single subsequence with $a_{t,n}\to a_t$ and $b_{t,n}\to b_t$ for every fixed $t$.
At the fixed factor $q_\star$, define the function of the angle
\[
 w_\star(\theta)=d(q_\star,\theta)
 +\sum_{t\geq1}a_t\bigl(u_t(q_\star,\theta)-d(q_\star,\theta)\bigr)
 +\sum_{t\geq1}b_tv_t(q_\star,\theta).
\]
Along the chosen subsequence, both $w_n(q_n,\theta)$ and $w_n(q_\star,\theta)$ converge to $w_\star(\theta)$ uniformly for $\theta\in[0,\pi]$.
Indeed, the bound with $j=0$ makes the sums over sufficiently large values of $t$ uniformly small, and each finite sum converges by coefficient convergence and continuity in $q$.
The limiting coefficient sums may be less than one because weights can move to larger and larger values of $t$ as $n$ increases.
The term $d$ outside the sums preserves their limiting contribution, since $u_t$ tends to $d$ and $v_t$ tends to zero as $t$ increases.
Passing to these limits in $w_n(q_n,\theta)<0$ and $\int w_n(q_\star,\theta)\,d\nu_\star\geq0$ gives
\[
 w_\star(\theta)\leq0\quad(0\leq\theta\leq\pi),
 \qquad \int w_\star(\theta)\,d\nu_\star\geq0.
\]
Since $w_\star$ is continuous and nonpositive, its nonnegative integral forces it to vanish on the support of $\nu_\star$.

At angle zero, writing $r=\sqrt q$ gives
\[
 u_t(q,0)=\frac{d_s(r)}{1+r^t},
 \qquad v_t(q,0)=-\frac{d_s(r)r^t}{1+r^t}.
\]
Since $r^t\leq r<1$ and $d_s(r)<0$, the two coefficient sums imply
$w_n(q,0)\leq d_s(r)(1-r)/(1+r)$.
Consequently,
\[
 w_\star(0)\leq d_s(\sqrt{q_\star})
 \frac{1-\sqrt{q_\star}}{1+\sqrt{q_\star}}<0.
\]

It remains to show that $w_\star$ has only finitely many zeros in $[0,\pi]$.
The same series defines $w_\star$ for every real $\theta$.
The derivative bound \eqref{eq:lag-geometric-tails} permits termwise differentiation of every order, uniformly on the real line.
Choose $b>0$ with $r_+e^b<1$.
Using $(t+2)^j\leq j!b^{-j}e^{b(t+2)}$ and summing the geometric series gives
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\mathbf R}|w_\star^{(j)}(\theta)|
 \leq c_0j!b^{-j},
 \qquad c_0=\frac{ce^{2b}}{1-r_+e^b}.
\]
For any real expansion point $\theta_0$, Taylor's theorem therefore gives
\[
 \left|w_\star(\theta)
 -\sum_{j=0}^m\frac{w_\star^{(j)}(\theta_0)}{j!}(\theta-\theta_0)^j\right|
 \leq c_0\left(\frac{|\theta-\theta_0|}{b}\right)^{m+1}.
\]
When $|\theta-\theta_0|<b$, the right-hand side tends to zero as $m\to\infty$, so the Taylor series equals $w_\star$ on this neighborhood.
The same radius $b$ works at every real expansion point.

Suppose that $w_\star$ has infinitely many distinct zeros in $[0,\pi]$.
By compactness, we can choose a strictly monotone sequence of these zeros converging to some $\theta_0\in[0,\pi]$, possibly an endpoint.
Between consecutive zeros, Rolle's theorem gives a zero of $w_\star'$.
These zeros also converge to $\theta_0$, and the same argument applies successively to every derivative.
By continuity, $w_\star^{(j)}(\theta_0)=0$ for every $j\geq0$.
The Taylor expansion then gives $w_\star(\theta)=0$ whenever $|\theta-\theta_0|<b$.
At every point inside this interval all derivatives vanish, so a Taylor expansion there gives another interval of radius $b$ on which $w_\star$ is zero.
Repeating with expansion points spaced $b/2$ apart toward zero eventually gives $w_\star(0)=0$, contradicting the strict inequality above.
Thus $w_\star$ has only finitely many zeros in $[0,\pi]$, and the support of $\nu_\star$ is finite.

label: lem:initialization-splice
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:initialization-splice}
Fix $s>1$ with $q_\star(s)>q_{\mathrm{quad}}(s)$, and set $\kappa=s^2$.
Consider any trajectory associated with a finitely supported optimal angular pair as in Section~\ref{sec:variational}.
After scaling this trajectory by a positive constant and adding one coordinate, it can be realized from iteration one onward by Nesterov's method on a single finite-dimensional objective in $\mathcal F_{1,\kappa}$.
The method starts with $x_{-1}=x_0$, and its squared-distance asymptotic factor is $q_\star(s)$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $\beta=\beta_\kappa\in(0,1)$ and set
\[
 a=\frac{\kappa}{1+\beta}=\frac{s(s+1)}2,
 \qquad
 p(v)=
 \begin{cases}
  a v^2/2,&v\geq0,\\
  \kappa v^2/2,&v\leq0.
 \end{cases}
\]
Since $1<a<\kappa$, this differentiable piecewise quadratic belongs to $\mathcal F_{1,\kappa}$.
Let $u_t$ and $v_t$ denote the scalar iterates and query points, respectively.
Starting NAG on $p$ from $u_{-1}=u_0=1$ gives
\[
 u_1=\frac{\beta}{1+\beta},\qquad u_t=0\quad(t\geq2).
\]
Indeed, the corresponding query points are
\[
 v_0=1,\qquad v_1=0,\qquad
 v_2=-\frac{\beta^2}{1+\beta},\qquad v_t=0\quad(t\geq3).
\]
The first gradient step gives $u_1$, the next extrapolation gives $v_1=0$, and every query $v\leq0$ is mapped to zero by the gradient step.

Write the interpolation condition \eqref{eq:ssc-interpolation} as $e_{ij}\leq0$, where
\[
 e_{ij}
 =f_j-f_i+\langle g_j,y_i-y_j\rangle
 +\frac{\|g_i-g_j\|^2}{2\kappa}
 +\frac{\kappa}{2(\kappa-1)}
 \left\|y_i-y_j-\frac{g_i-g_j}{\kappa}\right\|^2.
\]
Let $e_{ij}^p$ be this residual with $y_t=v_t$, $g_t=p'(v_t)$, and $f_t=p(v_t)$.
Every later query and the optimum satisfy $v_t\leq0$, with $v_\star=0$.
Substituting $(y_0,g_0,f_0)=(1,a,a/2)$ and $(y_t,g_t,f_t)=(v_t,\kappa v_t,\kappa v_t^2/2)$ gives
\[
 e^p_{0t}=-c+(\kappa-a)v_t\leq-c,
 \qquad e^p_{t0}=-c,
 \qquad
 c=\frac{(a-1)(\kappa-a)}{2(\kappa-1)}>0.
\]
Thus the inequalities for index pairs $(0,t)$ and $(t,0)$ have uniform slack $c$.
Pairs of later query points, including the optimum, have residual zero because $p(v)=\kappa v^2/2$ for $v\leq0$.

Use hats for all quantities associated with the prescribed trajectory, beginning at $t=1$.
The extrapolation equation requires
\[
 \widehat y_1
 =(1+\beta)\widehat x_1-\beta \widehat x_0,
\]
so set
\[
 \widehat x_0
 =\frac{(1+\beta)\widehat x_1-\widehat y_1}{\beta}.
\]
Set $\widehat x_{-1}=\widehat y_0=\widehat x_0$ and prescribe
\[
 \widehat g_0
 =\kappa(\widehat x_0-\widehat x_1).
\]
Then the first gradient step reaches $\widehat x_1$, and the next extrapolation gives $\widehat y_1$.
The NAG updates do not depend on $\widehat f_0$, so assign it any finite value.
Scaling the prescribed trajectory and adding the scalar coordinate will enforce the interpolation inequalities involving index $0$.

At the optimum, prescribe
\[
 (\widehat y_\star,\widehat g_\star,\widehat f_\star)
 =(0,0,0),
\]
which is compatible with the prescribed trajectory by the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:closed-rate-problem}.
The prescribed points and gradients are bounded because $q_\star(s)<1$.
The interpolation inequalities with the optimum imply
\[
 0\leq \widehat f_t
 \leq\langle \widehat g_t,\widehat y_t\rangle
 \leq\|\widehat g_t\|\|\widehat y_t\|.
\]
The prescribed function values are therefore bounded as well.
Since $\widehat y_0$, $\widehat g_0$, and $\widehat f_0$ are fixed, the interpolation residuals involving index $0$ are uniformly bounded:
\[
 b=\sup_{t\in\{\star,1,2,\ldots\}}
 \max\{0,\widehat e_{0t},\widehat e_{t0}\}<\infty.
\]

For $\varepsilon>0$, define the combined iterates, query points, gradients, and function values by
\[
 x_t=(u_t,\varepsilon \widehat x_t),
 \qquad
 y_t=(v_t,\varepsilon \widehat y_t),
\]
\[
 g_t=(p'(v_t),\varepsilon \widehat g_t),
 \qquad
 f_t=p(v_t)+\varepsilon^2\widehat f_t.
\]
At the optimum, set $(y_\star,g_\star,f_\star)=(0,0,0)$.
Inner products and squared norms add across coordinates, so
\[
 e_{ij}=e_{ij}^p+\varepsilon^2\widehat e_{ij}.
\]
For pairs with neither index equal to $0$, we have $\widehat e_{ij}\leq0$, and therefore $e_{ij}\leq0$.
Choose
\[
 \varepsilon^2=\frac{c}{b+1}.
\]
For every $t\in\{\star,1,2,\ldots\}$, this gives
\[
 \max\{e_{0t},e_{t0}\}
 \leq-c+\varepsilon^2b
 =-\frac{c}{b+1}<0.
\]
Together with $e_{00}=0$, this proves all the interpolation inequalities.

Summing the transformed interpolation inequalities around any finite cycle proves cyclic monotonicity of the entire countable set of pairs $(\sigma_i,r_i)$.
The construction in Section~\ref{sec:interpolation} therefore gives one function $f\in\mathcal F_{1,\kappa}$ with $\nabla f(y_i)=g_i$ at every prescribed query point, including the optimum.
This applies to the whole set at once and uses the same finite-dimensional space as the combined trajectory.

The constructed sequences satisfy the NAG updates \eqref{eq:nag} because $\nabla f(y_t)=g_t$.
Thus $(x_t)$ is the trajectory of Nesterov's method on $f$, with $x_{-1}=x_0$.
Interpolation at the origin gives $\nabla f(0)=0$, so $x_\star=0$.
The initial point is nonoptimal because its first coordinate is $u_0=1$.

Let $\theta_k$ be a support angle of the optimal measure and put $z_k=\sqrt{q_\star(s)}\,e^{i\theta_k}$.
The construction in Section~\ref{sec:rotating-trajectories} makes the corresponding component of $r_t$ proportional to $z_k^t$.
Since $x_{t+1}=(\kappa-1)r_t/\kappa$, the corresponding prescribed iterate, written as a complex number $\widehat x_{t,k}$, satisfies
\[
 \widehat x_{t,k}=z_k^{t-1}\widehat x_{1,k},
 \qquad
 |\widehat x_{t,k}|^2=q_\star(s)^{t-1}|\widehat x_{1,k}|^2,
 \qquad t\geq1.
\]
All $z_k$ have modulus $\sqrt{q_\star(s)}$, so the norm of each prescribed planar component contracts by this same factor.
The components occupy separate coordinates, so their squared norms add.
Including the additional scalar coordinate gives, for $t\geq1$,
\[
 \|x_t\|^2
 =u_t^2+\varepsilon^2\|\widehat x_t\|^2
 =u_t^2+\varepsilon^2q_\star(s)^{t-1}\|\widehat x_1\|^2.
\]
The vector $\widehat x_1$ is nonzero, and $u_t=0$ for every $t\geq2$.
Thus the additional coordinate contributes nothing to the squared distance from iteration two onward.
The positive scaling and the initial-distance normalization contribute only fixed factors, whose $t$th roots tend to one.
Taking $t$th roots therefore yields
\[
 \lim_{t\to\infty}
 \left(\frac{\|x_t-x_\star\|^2}{\|x_0-x_\star\|^2}\right)^{1/t}
 =q_\star(s).
\]

title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:strict-separator-rate}
Fix $s>1$ and $q>q_{\mathrm{quad}}(s)$.
Suppose a nonnegative linear combination of finitely many cycle costs is strictly negative at every angle $\theta\in[0,\pi]$.
Then there is a finite $b(s,q)$ such that every NAG trajectory \eqref{eq:nag} with $\kappa=s^2$, on any finite-dimensional objective $f\in\mathcal F_{1,s^2}$ and with any initialization $x_{-1}=x_0$, satisfies
\[
 \|x_t-x_\star\|^2\leq b(s,q)q^t\|x_0-x_\star\|^2,
 \qquad t\geq0.
\]

label: eq:inverse-transfer
title: Proof
body_md:
For $q>q_{\mathrm{quad}}(s)$, the coefficient $d_s(z)$ is nonzero on $|z|=\sqrt q$.
Define its reciprocal
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:inverse-transfer}
 p_s(z)=\frac1{d_s(z)}
 =-\frac{s^2z^2}{(s^2-1)(sz-(s-1))^2}.
\end{equation}
Multiplying both vectors in \eqref{eq:nag-transfer} by $p_s(z)$ changes the normalization from $r_t=z^t$ to $\sigma_t=z^t$.
All inner products are multiplied by the same positive factor:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:normalization-inner-product}
 \operatorname{Re}\bigl[p_s(z)z^i(\bar z^i-\bar z^j)\bigr]
 =|p_s(z)|^2c_{ij}(\theta).
\end{equation}
This change preserves the sign of every cycle separator.

Let $f$ be defined on $\mathbf R^d$.
Translate the minimizer to zero and set $f(0)=0$.
Write
\[
 c=(s^2-1)^{-1},\qquad
 a=\frac{1-1/s}{\sqrt q}\in(0,1),\qquad
 h(y)=f(y)-\frac12\|y\|^2.
\]
The function $h$ is convex, has gradient Lipschitz constant $s^2-1$, and satisfies $\nabla h(0)=0$.
For every sequence, use the scaling $\bar u_t=q^{-t/2}u_t$.
The gradient bound becomes
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:scaled-uncertainty}
 \bigl\|q^{-t/2}\nabla h(q^{t/2}v)\bigr\|
 \leq(s^2-1)\|v\|,
 \qquad v\in\mathbf R^d.
\end{equation}

For the NAG trajectory, set $\sigma_t=\nabla h(y_t)$.
Eliminating $x_t$ from the NAG equations gives, for $t\geq2$,
\[
 \bar y_t-2a\bar y_{t-1}+a^2\bar y_{t-2}
 =-2ca\bar\sigma_{t-1}+ca^2\bar\sigma_{t-2}.
\]
The standard initialization gives
\[
 \bar y_0=x_0,\qquad
 \bar y_1=a\left(1+\frac1{s+1}\right)x_0-2ca\bar\sigma_0.
\]
Expanding this recurrence yields, for $t\geq0$,
\[
 \bar y_t=e_t-c\sum_{j=1}^t(j+1)a^j\bar\sigma_{t-j},
 \qquad
 e_t=\left(1+\frac{t}{s+1}\right)a^t x_0.
\]
The sequence $e$ accounts for the initialization and solves the same recurrence with every $\sigma_t$ set to zero.

Let $\ell_2^d$ denote the space of square-summable $\mathbf R^d$-valued sequences indexed by $\mathbf Z$, with norm
\[
 \|u\|_{\ell_2}^2=\sum_{t\in\mathbf Z}\|u_t\|^2.
\]
Sequences defined only for $t\geq0$ are set to zero for $t<0$.
To abbreviate the weighted sum in the recurrence, define the linear map
\[
 g(u)_t=-c\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}(j+1)a^j u_{t-j},
 \qquad u\in\ell_2^d.
\]
Shifting the indices of a sequence preserves its $\ell_2$ norm.
The triangle inequality and the identity $\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}(j+1)a^j=(1-a)^{-2}-1$ therefore give
\[
 \|g(u)\|_{\ell_2}\leq c_g\|u\|_{\ell_2},
 \qquad c_g=c\bigl((1-a)^{-2}-1\bigr).
\]
For a sequence that vanishes at negative indices, the sum defining $g(u)_t$ has only $t$ possibly nonzero terms when $t\geq0$, and $g(u)_t=0$ when $t<0$.
Thus the same formula defines $g(u)$ without assuming square summability.
We will prove a bound for every square-summable sequence $e$ that vanishes at negative indices.
Allowing arbitrary $e$ will let us apply the same bound to the modified sequence used in the final induction.
For any such sequence and any scalar $\tau\in[0,1]$, consider
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:rescaled-recursion}
 \begin{aligned}
 \bar y_t&=e_t+g(\bar\sigma)_t
 =e_t-c\sum_{j=1}^t(j+1)a^j\bar\sigma_{t-j},\\
 \bar\sigma_t&=\tau q^{-t/2}\nabla h(q^{t/2}\bar y_t),
 \qquad t\geq0.
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
The NAG trajectory corresponds to $\tau=1$ and the initialization sequence $e$ derived above.
These equations determine a unique sequence by induction on $t$.
Each value of $\bar y_t$ depends only on the previously determined gradients.

To express the cycle inequalities, write
\[
 f_\tau(y)=\frac12\|y\|^2+\tau h(y).
\]
As $\tau$ varies from zero to one, this function interpolates between the quadratic $\|y\|^2/2$ and $f$.
For every $\tau\in[0,1]$, this function belongs to $\mathcal F_{1,s^2}$ and has minimizer zero.
For arbitrary query points, write $\sigma_t=\tau\nabla h(y_t)$, consistently with \eqref{eq:rescaled-recursion} after rescaling.
Take $y_t=\sigma_t=0$ for $t<0$.
Applying \eqref{eq:interpolation-variables} to $f_\tau$ gives $\sigma=\sigma_t$ and $r=y_t-c\sigma_t$ at each query point $y_t$.
For each selected cycle $\gamma=(n_0,\ldots,n_\ell=n_0)$, cyclic monotonicity therefore gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:local-cycle-supply}
 a_{\gamma,t}
 =\sum_{j=0}^{\ell-1}
 \langle y_{t+n_j}-c\sigma_{t+n_j},
 \sigma_{t+n_j}-\sigma_{t+n_{j+1}}\rangle\geq0,
 \qquad t\in\mathbf Z.
\end{equation}
The sum vanishes for $t<-\max_j n_j$.
After rescaling,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:scaled-local-supply}
 q^{-t}a_{\gamma,t}
 =\sum_{j=0}^{\ell-1}
 \left\langle q^{n_j/2}(\bar y_{t+n_j}-c\bar\sigma_{t+n_j}),
 q^{n_j/2}\bar\sigma_{t+n_j}
 -q^{n_{j+1}/2}\bar\sigma_{t+n_{j+1}}\right\rangle\geq0.
\end{equation}
As in alternative~2 of Lemma~\ref{lem:strict-alternative}, write $w_\gamma\geq0$ for the separator weights, with one weight for each selected cycle.
We collect terms according to the difference between their two iteration indices.
For example, replacing $t+n_j$ by $t$ pairs the first vector in \eqref{eq:scaled-local-supply} with $\bar\sigma_{t+n_{j+1}-n_j}$ in its second term.
The following finite sums record these index differences as powers of $z\neq0$:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:cycle-laurent-multiplier}
 k_\gamma(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{\ell-1}
 \left(q^{n_j}-q^{(n_j+n_{j+1})/2}z^{n_{j+1}-n_j}\right),
 \qquad
 k(z)=\sum_\gamma w_\gamma k_\gamma(z)=\sum_j k_jz^j.
\end{equation}
Only finitely many real coefficients $k_j$ are nonzero.
In sums involving these coefficients, indices without stated limits range over $\mathbf Z$.
Set $c_k=\sum_j|k_j|$.
Since each shift preserves the norm, the triangle inequality gives
\[
 \left\|\left(\sum_j k_ju_{t+j}\right)_{t\in\mathbf Z}\right\|_{\ell_2}
 \leq c_k\|u\|_{\ell_2}.
\]
For $\bar y\in\ell_2^d$, the gradient bound \eqref{eq:scaled-uncertainty} gives $\bar\sigma\in\ell_2^d$.
Each sum of shifted inner products then converges absolutely by Cauchy--Schwarz.
Summing \eqref{eq:scaled-local-supply} and reindexing therefore gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:summed-cycle-supply}
 \sum_{t,j}k_j\langle\bar y_t-c\bar\sigma_t,\bar\sigma_{t+j}\rangle
 =\sum_\gamma w_\gamma\sum_{t\in\mathbf Z}q^{-t}a_{\gamma,t}\geq0.
\end{equation}

For $z=\sqrt q\,e^{i\theta}$, direct substitution gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:strict-cycle-fdi}
 \operatorname{Re}\!\left[\overline{p_s(z)}k(e^{i\theta})\right]
 =|p_s(z)|^2\sum_\gamma w_\gamma c_\gamma(\theta)
 \leq-c_0
\end{equation}
for some $c_0>0$.
Continuity supplies this margin on $[0,\pi]$, and real coefficients extend it to the full unit circle.
Since $p_s(\sqrt q\,e^{i\theta})=-c/(1-ae^{-i\theta})^2$, clearing the denominator gives
\[
 c\operatorname{Re}\bigl[k(e^{i\theta})(1-ae^{-i\theta})^2\bigr]
 \geq c_0|1-ae^{-i\theta}|^4,
 \qquad \theta\in\mathbf R.
\]
We next turn this pointwise inequality into an inequality for sequences.
For any $u\in\ell_2^d$, define
\[
 v_t=u_t-2au_{t-1}+a^2u_{t-2}.
\]
We will show that
\[
 c\sum_{t,j}k_j\langle u_t,v_{t+j}\rangle
 \geq c_0\|v\|_{\ell_2}^2.
\]
First suppose that $u$ has finite support.
Multiplying the pointwise inequality by a squared norm shows that
\[
 \left\|\sum_tu_te^{-it\theta}\right\|^2
 \left(c\operatorname{Re}\bigl[k(e^{i\theta})(1-ae^{-i\theta})^2\bigr]
       -c_0|1-ae^{-i\theta}|^4\right)
\]
is nonnegative for every real $\theta$.
After expansion, this expression is a finite sum of terms proportional to $e^{ij\theta}$ with integer indices $j$.
Choose a positive integer $p$ larger than every $|j|$ occurring in this sum.
The finite geometric-sum identity
\[
 \frac1p\sum_{r=0}^{p-1}\exp(2\pi i r j/p)
 =\begin{cases}1,&j=0,\\0,&j\ne0,\end{cases}
 \qquad j\in\mathbf Z,\quad |j|<p,
\]
shows that averaging at $\theta=2\pi r/p$, for $r=0,\ldots,p-1$, keeps only the constant coefficient.
To identify that coefficient, note that $\sum_tv_te^{-it\theta}=(1-ae^{-i\theta})^2\sum_tu_te^{-it\theta}$.
In the product with $k(e^{i\theta})$, a term pairing $u_t$ with $v_r$ has factor $e^{i(t+j-r)\theta}$ and contributes to the constant coefficient exactly when $r=t+j$.
The average is therefore $c\sum_{t,j}k_j\langle u_t,v_{t+j}\rangle-c_0\|v\|_{\ell_2}^2$.
Every expression being averaged is nonnegative, so this proves the claimed sequence inequality for finite support.
Truncation extends the inequality to every square-summable $u$.
Indeed, the displayed bound for the weighted shifts and the inequality $\|v\|_{\ell_2}\leq(1+a)^2\|u\|_{\ell_2}$ make both quadratic expressions continuous.

Conversely, for any $v\in\ell_2^d$, the sequence
\[
 u_t=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}(j+1)a^jv_{t-j}
\]
has norm at most $(1-a)^{-2}\|v\|_{\ell_2}$ by the triangle inequality.
It satisfies $v_t=u_t-2au_{t-1}+a^2u_{t-2}$ by cancellation of the coefficients.
The coefficient of $v_t$ is one, the coefficient of $v_{t-1}$ is $2a-2a=0$, and every later coefficient is $\bigl((j+1)-2j+(j-1)\bigr)a^j=0$ for $j\geq2$.
The same definition gives $g(v)_t-cv_t=-cu_t$.
Consequently,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:cycle-convolution-coercivity}
 \sum_{t,j}k_j\langle g(v)_t-cv_t,v_{t+j}\rangle
 \leq-c_0\|v\|_{\ell_2}^2.
\end{equation}

Suppose temporarily that the sequence $\bar y$ generated by \eqref{eq:rescaled-recursion} is square summable for a given $e\in\ell_2^d$ and $\tau\in[0,1]$.
Substitute $\bar y=e+g(\bar\sigma)$ into \eqref{eq:summed-cycle-supply}.
The preceding inequality bounds the terms involving $g(\bar\sigma)-c\bar\sigma$.
Cauchy--Schwarz and the bound for the weighted shifts bound the remaining terms by $c_k\|e\|_{\ell_2}\|\bar\sigma\|_{\ell_2}$.
Thus
\[
 0\leq-c_0\|\bar\sigma\|_{\ell_2}^2
       +c_k\|e\|_{\ell_2}\|\bar\sigma\|_{\ell_2}.
\]
If $\|\bar\sigma\|_{\ell_2}>0$, divide by this norm and then use $\bar y=e+g(\bar\sigma)$.
If this norm is zero, the same bounds hold directly.
We obtain
\[
 \|\bar\sigma\|_{\ell_2}\leq\frac{c_k}{c_0}\|e\|_{\ell_2},
 \qquad
 \|\bar y\|_{\ell_2}\leq c_y\|e\|_{\ell_2},
 \qquad c_y=1+\frac{c_gc_k}{c_0}.
\]
Once the separator is fixed, these constants depend only on $s,q$.
In particular, they are independent of $\tau$, $e$, the objective, and the dimension.

We now remove this assumption by increasing $\tau$ from zero to one in finitely many steps.
Choose a positive integer $m>2c_yc_g(s^2-1)$ and set $\tau_j=j/m$ for $j=0,\ldots,m$.
We prove by induction on $j$ that, for every square-summable $e$ vanishing at negative indices, the sequence $\bar y$ generated by \eqref{eq:rescaled-recursion} at $\tau=\tau_j$ satisfies
\[
 \sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\|\bar y_t\|^2<\infty.
\]

\emph{Base case.}
At $\tau_0=0$, we have $\bar\sigma=0$ and $\bar y=e$, so the claim holds.

\emph{Induction step.}
Fix $1\leq j\leq m$ and assume the claim holds at $\tau_{j-1}$.
Fix any allowed $e$ and let $\bar y$ be the sequence at $\tau_j$.
We will bound $\sum_{t=0}^n\|\bar y_t\|^2$ independently of $n$.
For each integer $n\geq0$, define
\[
 u_t^{(n)}=
 \begin{cases}
  q^{-t/2}\nabla h(q^{t/2}\bar y_t),&0\leq t\leq n,\\
  0,&\text{otherwise},
 \end{cases}
 \qquad
 e^{(n)}=e+\frac1m g(u^{(n)}).
\]
Only finitely many terms of $u^{(n)}$ are nonzero, so the bound on $g$ makes $e^{(n)}$ square summable.
It also vanishes at negative indices.
The induction hypothesis therefore gives a square-summable sequence $\bar y^{(n)}$ at $\tau_{j-1}$ with $e^{(n)}$ in place of $e$.

The modification of $e$ makes the first $n+1$ terms of these two sequences agree.
Indeed, $g(u)_t$ uses only terms with indices less than $t$, so for $0\leq t\leq n$,
\[
 \bar y_t=e_t+\tau_jg(u^{(n)})_t
 =e_t^{(n)}+\tau_{j-1}g(u^{(n)})_t.
\]
The last equality uses $\tau_j=\tau_{j-1}+1/m$.
These are exactly the recurrence equations at $\tau_{j-1}$ with $e^{(n)}$ through time $n$.
They determine each term from the previous ones, so $\bar y_t^{(n)}=\bar y_t$ for $0\leq t\leq n$.

Since $\bar y^{(n)}$ is square summable, the preceding norm estimate applies to it.
Combining that estimate with the bound on $g$ and \eqref{eq:scaled-uncertainty} gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \left(\sum_{t=0}^n\|\bar y_t\|^2\right)^{1/2}
 &\leq\|\bar y^{(n)}\|_{\ell_2}
 \leq c_y\|e^{(n)}\|_{\ell_2}\\
 &\leq c_y\|e\|_{\ell_2}
 +\frac{c_yc_g(s^2-1)}m
  \left(\sum_{t=0}^n\|\bar y_t\|^2\right)^{1/2}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
The coefficient multiplying the partial norm on the right is less than $1/2$.
Moving this term to the left gives, for every $n$,
\[
 \left(\sum_{t=0}^n\|\bar y_t\|^2\right)^{1/2}
 \leq2c_y\|e\|_{\ell_2}.
\]
Every partial sum of squared norms is therefore at most $4c_y^2\|e\|_{\ell_2}^2$.
These partial sums are nondecreasing and bounded, so their limit is finite.
This proves the claim at $\tau_j$ and completes the induction.

At $\tau_m=1$, the sequence $\bar y$ is square summable, and the gradient bound gives $\bar\sigma\in\ell_2^d$.
The earlier estimates for both sequences now apply and yield
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:scaled-loop-gain}
 \|\bar y\|_{\ell_2}^2+\|\bar\sigma\|_{\ell_2}^2
 \leq\left(c_y^2+\frac{c_k^2}{c_0^2}\right)\|e\|_{\ell_2}^2.
\end{equation}

Return to the NAG initialization sequence $e$ derived above.
Since $a<1$, the squared norm $\|e\|_{\ell_2}^2$ is a finite multiple of $\|x_0\|^2$ depending only on $s,q$.
Finally, $s^2x_{t+1}=(s^2-1)y_t-\sigma_t$ gives
\[
 q^{-(t+1)}\|x_{t+1}\|^2
 \leq\frac{(s^2-1)^2+1}{s^4q}
 \left(\|\bar y\|_{\ell_2}^2+\|\bar\sigma\|_{\ell_2}^2\right).
\]
Combining this with \eqref{eq:scaled-loop-gain} gives a finite constant $b_1(s,q)$ such that
\[
 \|x_t\|^2\leq b_1(s,q)q^t\|x_0\|^2,
 \qquad t\geq1.
\]
Set $b(s,q)=\max\{1,b_1(s,q)\}$.
Since $b(s,q)\geq b_1(s,q)$, the bound still holds for every $t\geq1$.
At $t=0$, we have $q^0=1$ and $b(s,q)\geq1$, so the bound reduces to $\|x_0\|^2\leq b(s,q)\|x_0\|^2$, which also holds.

The proof used coordinates centered at the minimizer.
Thus the vectors denoted above by $x_t$ and $x_0$ are $x_t-x_\star$ and $x_0-x_\star$ in the original coordinates.
The bound in those coordinates is therefore
\[
 \|x_t-x_\star\|^2\leq b(s,q)q^t\|x_0-x_\star\|^2,
 \qquad t\geq0,
\]
as claimed.

title: Remark
body_md:
For $f\in\mathcal F_{1,1}$, strong convexity and smoothness at the minimizer give
\[
 \frac12\|x-x_\star\|^2
 \leq f(x)-f(x_\star)
 \leq\frac12\|x-x_\star\|^2.
\]
Hence $f(x)=f(x_\star)+\frac12\|x-x_\star\|^2$ and $\nabla f(x)=x-x_\star$ for every $x$.
When $\kappa=1$, the momentum coefficient is $\beta_1=0$ and the step size is one.
Thus $x_{t+1}=x_t-\nabla f(x_t)=x_\star$ for every $t\geq0$.
Both asymptotic factors in \eqref{eq:rho-fix}--\eqref{eq:rho-hor} are therefore zero.
head: environment
name: The case $\kappa=1$

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $\kappa>1$ and set $s=\sqrt\kappa$.
Proposition~\ref{prop:fixed-domain-rate} gives
\[
 q_{\mathrm{quad}}(s)\leqq_\star(s)\leq1-1/s<1.
\]
We first prove $q_\star(s)\leq\rho_{\mathrm{fix}}(s^2)$ by constructing one fixed objective and initial point that attain $q_\star(s)$.

If $q_\star(s)=q_{\mathrm{quad}}(s)$, the scalar quadratic $f(x)=x^2/2$ attains this factor from any nonzero standard initialization by \eqref{eq:q0}.

Suppose $q_\star(s)>q_{\mathrm{quad}}(s)$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:finite-optimal-support} supplies a pair $(\nu_\star,\varphi_0^\star)$ satisfying \eqref{eq:star-feasible} at $q=q_\star(s)$, with $\nu_\star$ supported on finitely many angles.
The associated contracting and rotating trajectory uses at most two real coordinates per support angle, so it is finite-dimensional.
By Lemma~\ref{lem:stars}, the corresponding interpolation values can be chosen as $\varphi_t=q_\star(s)^t\varphi_0^\star$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:initialization-splice} then gives a single objective in $\mathcal F_{1,s^2}$ and an initialization $x_{-1}=x_0\neq x_\star$ whose NAG trajectory has asymptotic squared-distance factor $q_\star(s)$.

Thus in both cases,
\[
 q_\star(s)\leq\rho_{\mathrm{fix}}(s^2)\leq\rho_{\mathrm{hor}}(s^2).
\]

For the upper bound, fix any $q\in(q_\star(s),1)$.
Since $q_\star(s)=\max\mathcal Q(s)$ by \eqref{eq:qcyc}, the interpolation conditions \eqref{eq:star-feasible} are infeasible at this $q$.
By Lemma~\ref{lem:stars}, no probability measure on $[0,\pi]$ satisfies all finite-cycle inequalities.
The equivalence following Lemma~\ref{lem:strict-alternative} rules out alternative~1, so alternative~2 gives a nonnegative combination of finitely many cycle costs that is strictly negative at every angle.

Since $q>q_{\mathrm{quad}}(s)$, Proposition~\ref{prop:strict-separator-rate} gives a finite $b(s,q)\geq1$ that depends only on $s,q$.
Taking the supremum over objectives, dimensions, and initial points yields
\[
 \sup_{d\geq1}\sup_{f\in\mathcal F_{1,s^2}(\mathbf R^d)}
 \sup_{x_0\neq x_\star}R_t(f,x_0)
 \leq b(s,q)q^t,
 \qquad t\geq0.
\]
Taking $t$th roots and the limit superior, with $q$ fixed, gives
\[
 \rho_{\mathrm{hor}}(s^2)\leq\lim_{t\to\infty}b(s,q)^{1/t}q=q.
\]

This holds for every $q\in(q_\star(s),1)$, so letting $q\downarrowq_\star(s)$ gives $\rho_{\mathrm{hor}}(s^2)\leqq_\star(s)$.
The constant $b(s,q)$ need not remain bounded as $q\downarrowq_\star(s)$, since the limit in $t$ was taken first.
Combining this upper bound with the lower bound proves \eqref{eq:main} for $\kappa>1$.

The bounds in \eqref{eq:qcyc} follow from the quadratic example and the inequality comparing iterations $0$ and $2$ in Lemma~\ref{lem:closed-rate-problem}.
Substituting $q_{\mathrm{quad}}(s)=(1-1/s)^2$ and $s=\sqrt\kappa$ gives \eqref{eq:classical-bracket}.
Both bounds tend to zero as $\kappa\downarrow1$ and to one as $\kappa\to\infty$, so $q_\star(\sqrt\kappa)$ has the same limits.
head: environment

label: eq:log-asymptotic
title: Proof
body_md:
Write $s=\sqrt\kappa$.
The quadratic lower bound in \eqref{eq:classical-bracket} already implies $q_\star(s)\to1$, so it suffices to prove
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:log-asymptotic}
 \lim_{s\to\infty}-s\logq_\star(s)=\frac43.
\end{equation}
We first show that, for each fixed $0<\lambda<4/3$ and all sufficiently large $s$, no $q\in[e^{-\lambda/s},1)$ is feasible for \eqref{eq:star-feasible}.
We then construct a feasible measure at $q=e^{-2\alpha/s}$ for each fixed $2/3<\alpha<3/4$ and all sufficiently large $s$.
These give upper and lower bounds on $q_\star(s)$, respectively, and the inequalities reverse for $-s\logq_\star(s)$.

\paragraph{Upper bound.}
Fix $q\in(q_{\mathrm{quad}}(s),1)$ and a pair $(\nu,\varphi_0)$ satisfying \eqref{eq:star-feasible}.
Because $d_s(z)$ is bounded on $|z|=\sqrt q<1$, the terms in \eqref{eq:edge-cost} defining $c_{t0}(\theta)$ tend to zero uniformly in $\theta$ as $t\to\infty$.
Hence $\bar c_{t0}(\nu)\to0$, so the lower inequality in \eqref{eq:star-feasible} gives $\varphi_0\geq0$ in the limit.
The upper inequality with $t=1$ then gives $\bar c_{01}(\nu)\geq0$.
Put $r=\sqrt q$ and $x=2r\cos\theta\in[-2r,2r]$.
Equations \eqref{eq:nag-transfer} and \eqref{eq:edge-cost} give
\[
 c_{01}(\theta)=-\frac{s^2-1}{2s^2q^2}\psi_s(q,x),
\]
where
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:lag-one-quadratic}
 \psi_s(q,x)=(s-1)^2x^2-q(qs^2+3s^2-4s+1)x
              +6q^2s^2-4q^2s-2qs^2+4qs-2q.
\end{equation}
Its unconstrained minimizer and value at the right endpoint are
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:lag-one-vertex}
 x_{\rm v}=\frac{q(qs^2+3s^2-4s+1)}{2(s-1)^2},
 \qquad
 \psi_s(q,2r)=2q(1-r)(sr-s+1)^2>0.
\end{equation}
If $x_{\rm v}\geq2r$, the minimum of $\psi_s(q,x)$ over $[-2r,2r]$ is its value at the right endpoint, which is positive by \eqref{eq:lag-one-vertex}.
Hence $c_{01}(\theta)<0$ for every angle, contradicting $\bar c_{01}(\nu)\geq0$.
Fix $0<\lambda<4/3$.
At $q=e^{-\lambda/s}$,
\[
 s(2\sqrt q-x_{\rm v})\longrightarrow\frac{3\lambda}{2}-2<0.
\]
Since $3\lambda/2-2<0$, the displayed limit implies $x_{\rm v}>2r$ at $q=e^{-\lambda/s}$ for all sufficiently large $s$.
To cover every larger $q<1$, write the condition $x_{\rm v}\geq2r$ as
\[
 r(r^2s^2+3s^2-4s+1)-4(s-1)^2\geq0.
\]
Its left-hand side is strictly increasing in $r$ for $s>1$, so the condition also holds for every $q\in[e^{-\lambda/s},1)$.
Since $e^{-\lambda/s}>q_{\mathrm{quad}}(s)$ for all sufficiently large $s$, the preceding argument rules out feasibility throughout this interval.
Therefore $q_\star(s)\leq e^{-\lambda/s}$ and $-s\logq_\star(s)\geq\lambda$.
Taking the limit inferior as $s\to\infty$ and then letting $\lambda\uparrow4/3$ gives
\[
 \liminf_{s\to\infty}-s\logq_\star(s)\geq\frac43.
\]
The same asymptotic upper bound follows from Gannot's result~\cite[Proposition~2.13]{gannot2022frequency}.

\paragraph{Lower bound.}
Fix $2/3<\alpha<3/4$ and set $r=e^{-\alpha/s}$ and $q=r^2$.
We seek a probability measure $\nu$ on $[0,\pi]$ such that $\bar c_{t0}(\nu)\geq0$ and $\bar c_{0t}(\nu)\geq0$ for every integer $t\geq1$.
Then \eqref{eq:star-feasible} holds with $\varphi_0=0$.
For $0<h<r$, let $\nu$ be the probability measure on $[0,\pi]$ with density
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:rational-circle-measure}
 \frac{(1-h^2)^5}{\pi(1+4h^2+h^4)|1-he^{i\theta}|^6}.
\end{equation}

This density gives explicit formulas for the two integrals needed to check feasibility.
Write $z=re^{i\theta}$ and $m_s=\int\operatorname{Re}\overline{d_s(z)}\,d\nu$.
Equation \eqref{eq:edge-cost} gives
\begin{align*}
 \bar c_{t0}(\nu)&=q^t m_s-\int\operatorname{Re}\left[\overline{d_s(z)}z^t\right]\,d\nu,\\
 \bar c_{0t}(\nu)&=m_s-\int\operatorname{Re}\left[\overline{d_s(z)}\bar z^t\right]\,d\nu.
\end{align*}
The subscripts $1$ and $2$ below correspond to the integrals containing $z^t$ and $\bar z^t$ in these two costs, respectively.
To evaluate them, use the absolutely convergent series
\[
 (1-he^{i\theta})^{-3}
 =\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\binom{k+2}{2}h^ke^{ik\theta}.
\]
Substitute this series and its complex conjugate into the density, and use \eqref{eq:nag-transfer}.
After taking real parts, all nonconstant terms integrate to zero because $\int_0^\pi\cos(j\theta)\,d\theta=0$ for every nonzero integer $j$.
With
\begin{align*}
 \delta={}&s^2r^2(h^4+4h^2+1)
 -6sr(s-1)h(h^2+1)+6(s-1)^2h^2,\\
 e_1={}&sr-(s-1)h,
 &e_2={}&srh-(s-1),
\end{align*}
this gives
\[
 m_s=-\frac{(s^2-1)\delta}{s^2r^2(1+4h^2+h^4)}.
\]
For $\delta\ne0$ and every integer $t\geq0$, we obtain
\begin{align}
 \int\operatorname{Re}\left[\overline{d_s(z)}z^t\right]\,d\nu
 &=m_s(rh)^t\left(1+a_1t+b_1\binom{t}{2}\right),\notag\\
 \int\operatorname{Re}\left[\overline{d_s(z)}\bar z^t\right]\,d\nu
 &=m_s(rh)^t\left(1+a_2t+b_2\binom{t}{2}\right),
\label{eq:rational-circle-moments}
\end{align}
where the coefficients are
\begin{align*}
 a_1&=-\frac{(h^2-1)e_1
 [(s-1)h^3+srh^2-4(s-1)h+2sr]}{\delta},
 &b_1&=\frac{(h^2-1)^2e_1^2}{\delta},\\
 a_2&=-\frac{(h^2-1)e_2
 [srh^2-3(s-1)h+2sr]}{h\delta},
 &b_2&=\frac{(h^2-1)^2e_2^2}{h^2\delta}.
\end{align*}
To satisfy \eqref{eq:star-feasible} with $\varphi_0=0$, it suffices to have
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:coefficient-tests}
 m_s>0,\qquad
 a_1\leq r/h-1,\qquad
 a_2\leq1/(rh)-1.
\end{equation}
Indeed, $m_s>0$ implies $\delta<0$, and hence $b_1\leq0$ and $b_2\leq0$.
For $u\geq0$, $a\leq u$, and $b\leq0$, Bernoulli's inequality gives
\[
 1+at+b\binom{t}{2}\leq1+ut\leq(1+u)^t,
 \qquad t=0,1,\ldots.
\]
Apply this with $u=r/h-1$ and $u=1/(rh)-1$, respectively.
The first integral in \eqref{eq:rational-circle-moments} is then at most $m_s q^t$, and the second is at most $m_s$.
Thus both averaged costs are nonnegative for every integer $t\geq1$.

We now choose $h$ to satisfy \eqref{eq:coefficient-tests}.
Write $\epsilon=1/s$ and $h=e^{-\eta\epsilon}$, and define the two slacks
\[
 g_1=r/h-1-a_1,\qquad
 g_2=1/(rh)-1-a_2.
\]
We will choose $\eta$ so that these slacks are equal and positive.
Set
\[
 \gamma=\sqrt{\frac{3\alpha(1-\alpha)^2}{3\alpha-2}}.
\]
The function $g(\epsilon,\eta)=(g_1-g_2)/\epsilon$ extends smoothly to a neighborhood of $(0,\gamma)$, with
\[
 g(0,\eta)=-2\,
 \frac{3\alpha(1-\alpha)^2-(3\alpha-2)\eta^2}
 {3\alpha^2-6\alpha-\eta^2+3}.
\]
Our choice of $\gamma$ gives $g(0,\gamma)=0$, and
\[
 \partial_\eta g(0,\gamma)
 =\frac{4(3\alpha-2)\gamma}
 {3\alpha^2-6\alpha-\gamma^2+3}\ne0.
\]
The denominator equals $6(\alpha-1)^3/(3\alpha-2)<0$.
The implicit function theorem therefore gives a smooth choice $\gamma_s=\gamma+O(s^{-1})$ for which $g_1=g_2$ when $\eta=\gamma_s$.
For this choice, Taylor expansion gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:circle-gap-expansions}
 g_1=g_2=\frac{\alpha}{2(3\alpha-2)}s^{-2}+O(s^{-3}).
\end{equation}
The same substitution gives
\[
 m_s\longrightarrow
 -\frac{3\alpha^2-6\alpha-\gamma^2+3}{3}
 =\frac{2(1-\alpha)^3}{3\alpha-2}>0.
\]
Thus $m_s$ and both slacks are positive for all sufficiently large $s$.
Also, $\gamma^2-\alpha^2=\alpha(3-4\alpha)/(3\alpha-2)>0$, so $\gamma>\alpha$.
Consequently, $h=e^{-\gamma_s/s}$ satisfies $0<h<r<1$ for all sufficiently large $s$.
Since $\alpha<1$, we have $r=e^{-\alpha/s}>1-\alpha/s>1-1/s$, so $q>q_{\mathrm{quad}}(s)$.
The measure $\nu$ therefore satisfies \eqref{eq:star-feasible} with $\varphi_0=0$ at $q=e^{-2\alpha/s}$ for all sufficiently large $s$.
Hence $q_\star(s)\geq e^{-2\alpha/s}$, which gives
\[
 \limsup_{s\to\infty}-s\logq_\star(s)\leq2\alpha.
\]
Letting $\alpha\downarrow2/3$ and combining with the upper bound proves \eqref{eq:log-asymptotic}.
Since $(-\log u)/(1-u)\to1$ as $u\uparrow1$, this is equivalent to \eqref{eq:large-kappa}.
The square-root expansion follows from $\sqrt{1-v}=1-v/2+o(v)$.

title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Support and equality conditions at the optimal factor

title: Proof
body_md:
Feasibility says that the average of every cycle cost is nonnegative, so the average of $\phi_\star$ is nonnegative as well.
If $\nu_\star$ has finite support, as in Lemma~\ref{lem:finite-optimal-support}, write $\nu_\star=\sum_{j=1}^m a_j\delta_{\theta_j}$ with $a_j>0$.
Then
\[
 0\leq\sum_{j=1}^m a_j\phi_\star(\theta_j)\leq0.
\]
Every summand is nonpositive, so $\phi_\star(\theta_j)=0$ for every $j$.
For a general feasible measure, we likewise have $0\leq\int\phi_\star\,d\nu_\star\leq0$.
If $\phi_\star$ were negative at a point in its support, continuity would give a neighborhood of positive measure on which it is bounded above by a negative number.
Since $\phi_\star\leq0$ everywhere, this would make its integral negative.
Thus \eqref{eq:contact-support} holds.

For the matrix condition, set $x_\theta=(e^{i\theta}I-A)^{-1}Ba$.
Then $Ax_\theta+Ba=e^{i\theta}x_\theta$ and $Cx_\theta+Da=H_\star(e^{i\theta})a$.
In the quadratic form defined by $K_\star(P)$, the state contribution is $(|e^{i\theta}|^2-1)x_\theta^*Px_\theta=0$.
The same cycle calculation as in \eqref{eq:strict-cycle-fdi} therefore gives
\[
 \begin{split}
 h_\theta(a)^*K_\star(P)h_\theta(a)
 &=a^*H_\star(e^{i\theta})^*M_\star H_\star(e^{i\theta})a\\
 &=|p_s(\sqrt q\,e^{i\theta})|^2
   \phi_\star(\theta)\|a\|^2=0.
 \end{split}
\]
Since $-K_\star(P)$ is positive semidefinite, a zero quadratic value implies that $h_\theta(a)$ lies in its kernel.
This proves \eqref{eq:contact-kyp-kernel}.

head: environment
name: An optimal solution requiring two components

label: eq:normalization-change
title: Proof
body_md:
We state the exact certificate in the normalization $\sigma_t=z^t$, as in Appendix~\ref{app:uniform-upper-bound}.
If $(\eta,v)$ denotes angular weights and the initial interpolation value in this normalization, the original normalization is
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:normalization-change}
 d\nu=\frac{|p_s(z)|^2\,d\eta}{\int|p_s(z)|^2\,d\eta},
 \qquad \varphi_0=\frac{v}{\int|p_s(z)|^2\,d\eta}.
\end{equation}
The inverse uses $|d_s(z)|^2$ in the same way.
Both weights are continuous and strictly positive, so these transformations preserve supports and every interpolation inequality.
Let
\[
 \xi_\star\doteq(q_{100},v_\star,w_\star,
 \chi_{1\star},\chi_{2\star},\lambda_{49},\lambda_{63},\lambda_{64})
\]
be the unique zero in the rational box of radius $10^{-58}$ around
\begin{align*}
 q_{100}&=0.859899778052548365740446035906789693\ldots,\\
 v_\star&=0.002854749733611906316731334872665651\ldots,\\
 w_\star&=0.432893789374821564486049487863967595\ldots,\\
 \chi_{1\star}&=1.847585923705342323643049369488243114\ldots,\\
 \chi_{2\star}&=1.833337063888573702334307789415459859\ldots.
\end{align*}
Here $\chi_j\doteq2\sqrt q\cos\theta_j$ is a \emph{real frequency coordinate}.  The
corresponding angles are
\[
 \theta_1=0.08709509851058300453\ldots,
 \qquad
 \theta_2=0.15162655445126233148\ldots,
\]
and the certificate measure is
$\eta_\star\doteq w_\star\delta_{\theta_1}
 +(1-w_\star)\delta_{\theta_2}$.
The optimal angular pair $(\nu_\star,\varphi_0^\star)$ satisfying \eqref{eq:star-feasible} at $q=q_{100}$ is obtained from $(\eta_\star,v_\star)$ by \eqref{eq:normalization-change}.

To specify the algebraic system, fix $s=\sqrt{100}=10$ and define, for integers $m\geq1$,
\[
 L_m(q,\chi)\doteq-\frac{|p_{10}(z)|^2c_{m0}(\theta)}{1-q^m},\qquad
 U_m(q,\chi)\doteq \frac{|p_{10}(z)|^2c_{0m}(\theta)}{1-q^m},
\]
where $z=\sqrt q\,e^{i\theta}$, $\theta=\arccos(\chi/(2\sqrt q))$, and
$c_{ij}$ is from \eqref{eq:edge-cost} at $s=10$.
Write
\[
 \langle A\rangle_w\doteq wA(q,\chi_1)+(1-w)A(q,\chi_2),
\]
and set
\[
 \Phi_{100}(q,\chi)\doteq\lambda_{49}L_{49}(q,\chi)
 +\lambda_{63}L_{63}(q,\chi)
 +\lambda_{64}L_{64}(q,\chi)-U_1(q,\chi).
\]
Dependence on the dual weights is suppressed in $\Phi_{100}$; derivatives
with respect to $\chi$ keep those weights fixed.
The eight equations are
\begin{gather}
 \langle U_1\rangle_w=v,
 \qquad
 \langle L_{49}\rangle_w=
 \langle L_{63}\rangle_w=
 \langle L_{64}\rangle_w=v,
\label{eq:k100-primal-system}\\
 \lambda_{49}+\lambda_{63}+\lambda_{64}=1,
 \qquad
 \Phi_{100}(q,\chi_1)=\partial_\chi\Phi_{100}(q,\chi_1)=\partial_\chi\Phi_{100}(q,\chi_2)=0.
\label{eq:k100-dual-system}
\end{gather}
The omitted equality $\Phi_{100}(q,\chi_2)=0$ follows from
\eqref{eq:k100-primal-system} and the positive component weights.  An
interval Krawczyk inclusion proves existence and uniqueness of the root in
the rational box.  All three dual weights are positive and equal
approximately to
\[
 (\lambda_{49},\lambda_{63},\lambda_{64})
 \approx ( 0.7275254636036373,\ 0.0389115479752263,\
   0.2335629884211364).
\]

Figure~\ref{fig:k100-tangency} plots $\chi\mapsto\Phi_{100}(q_{100},\chi)$, keeping the
three dual multipliers fixed at the same algebraic solution. Its two contacts
correspond to the two rotation angles above.
\begin{figure}[tbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/nag_kappa100_tangency.pdf}
\caption{Numerical illustration of $\Phi_{100}(q_{100},\chi)$ with $q$ and the dual
multipliers fixed. Left: the full allowed interval
$[-2\sqrt{q_{100}},2\sqrt{q_{100}}]$.
Right: enlargement of the shaded region, showing both contacts
$\chi_{1\star}$ and $\chi_{2\star}$, labeled by their rotation angles
$\theta_j=\arccos(\chi_{j\star}/(2\sqrt{q_{100}}))$.}
\label{fig:k100-tangency}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{The four-dimensional self-similar tail.}
Set
\[
 z_j\doteq\frac{\chi_{j\star}}2
 +i\sqrt{q_{100}-\frac{\chi_{j\star}^2}{4}},
 \qquad a_1\doteq\sqrt{w_\star},
 \qquad a_2\doteq\sqrt{1-w_\star}.
\]
Thus $|z_1|^2=|z_2|^2=q_{100}$.  In $\mathbb C^2\cong\mathbf R^4$, define
\begin{align}
 \sigma_t&\doteq(a_1z_1^t,a_2z_2^t),\notag\\
 r_t&\doteq(a_1p_{10}(z_1)z_1^t,
        a_2p_{10}(z_2)z_2^t),
 &x_{t+1}&\doteq\frac{99}{100}r_t,
 \qquad t\in\mathbb Z,\notag\\
 y_t&\doteq r_t+\frac1{99}\sigma_t,
 &g_t&\doteq y_t+\sigma_t,
 \qquad t\geq0.
\label{eq:k100-tail}
\end{align}
Here $p_{10}$ means \eqref{eq:inverse-transfer} with $s=10$.  Its definition makes these
identities exactly consistent with the Nesterov momentum and gradient steps.  In particular,
\begin{equation}
 \frac{\|x_{t+1}\|^2}{\|x_1\|^2}=q_{100}^t,
 \qquad t\geq0.
\label{eq:k100-exact-decay}
\end{equation}
The four eigenvalues $z_1,\bar z_1,z_2,\bar z_2$ are pairwise distinct and
all four modal coefficients are nonzero.  The associated four-column
Vandermonde determinant is therefore nonzero, so the real span of the tail is
exactly four-dimensional.
For completeness, with the objective minimum normalized to $f(0)=0$, the
corresponding function values can be taken as
\begin{equation}
 f_t\doteq\langle\sigma_t,y_t\rangle-q_{100}^tv_\star
 -\frac1{198}\|\sigma_t\|^2+\frac12\|y_t\|^2.
\label{eq:k100-values}
\end{equation}
Indeed, with $\varphi(0)=0$, Lemma~\ref{lem:stars} allows the interpolation
values $\varphi_t=q_{100}^t v_\star$ in the normalization of
\eqref{eq:k100-tail}. They satisfy
\[
 \varphi_i-\varphi_j\leq\langle r_i,\sigma_i-\sigma_j\rangle
\]
for every ordered pair, including comparisons with the optimum.
There is therefore a proper closed convex function $\varphi$ with
$\varphi(\sigma_t)=\varphi_t$ and $r_t\in\partial\varphi(\sigma_t)$ for every $t$.
Reversing the transform \eqref{eq:phi} then gives \eqref{eq:k100-values},
so the entire sequence of query points, gradients, and function values comes
from one function in $\mathcal F_{1,100}(\mathbf R^4)$.

\paragraph{Why two components are necessary.}
As in the case for $\kappa=10$ in Appendix~\ref{app:kappa-ten},
we exactly check the two interpolation inequalities for each index
$m=1,\ldots,180$ and then use geometric bounds for both families at larger
indices. Equality holds only in the upper inequality at $m=1$ and the
lower inequalities at $m=49,63,64$. The interval calculation also proves the global
factorization
\[
 \Phi_{100}(q_{100},\chi)=
 \frac{(\chi-\chi_{1\star})^2(\chi-\chi_{2\star})^2R_{62}(\chi)}{D(\chi)},
 \qquad
 \frac{R_{62}(\chi)}{D(\chi)}>0,
 \quad |\chi|\leq2\sqrt{q_{100}}.
\]
For any feasible angular measure $\nu$ at $q=q_{100}$, the corresponding angular measure $\eta$ from \eqref{eq:normalization-change} satisfies
$\int\Phi_{100}(q_{100},\chi(\theta))\,d\eta(\theta)\leq0$, while the factorization gives
$\Phi_{100}(q_{100},\chi)\geq0$.  We call its two zeros the \emph{contact
frequencies}, because the dual inequality is tight there.  Such a measure must
therefore be supported on these two frequencies, and the change of weights preserves support.  Neither contact works
alone: directed interval arithmetic proves
\begin{align*}
 L_{56}(q_{100},\chi_{1\star})
 -U_1(q_{100},\chi_{1\star})
 &>0.00511062771457,\\
 L_{35}(q_{100},\chi_{2\star})
 -U_1(q_{100},\chi_{2\star})
 &>0.0281844327967.
\end{align*}
Each singleton therefore has an empty feasible interval for $\varphi_0$.  Every
optimal angular measure consequently has support cardinality exactly two, not
merely at most two. This counts angles in $[0,\pi]$; a disk measure may split
the mass at each angle between conjugate points.

For the matching upper bound, let $C_m^\sigma(q,\chi)$ be the cost of the
cycle $(0,1,\ldots,m,0)$ for $\sigma_t=z^t$ and $r_t=p_{10}(z)z^t$.
Summing its consecutive comparisons and its closing comparison gives
\[
 C_m^\sigma(q,\chi)=(1-q^m)\bigl(U_1(q,\chi)-L_m(q,\chi)\bigr).
\]
With $q=r^2$, define
\[
 S(r,\theta)\doteq
 \sum_{m\in\{49,63,64\}}\frac{\lambda_m}{1-q_{100}^m}
 C_m^\sigma(r^2,2r\cos\theta).
\]
The coefficients $\lambda_m/(1-q_{100}^m)$ are positive and independent of $r$.
They are the cycle weights $w_\gamma$ of Appendix~\ref{app:uniform-upper-bound} for $\gamma=(0,1,\ldots,m,0)$, whereas $w_\star$ and $1-w_\star$ weight the two angles.
At $r=\sqrt{q_{100}}$, $S(r,\theta)=-\Phi_{100}(q_{100},2r\cos\theta)$.
Set
\[
 N(r,\theta) \doteq 99\lvert10re^{i\theta}-9\rvert^4S(r,\theta).
\]
The multiplicative factor is positive on the relevant rectangle.  At
$r=\sqrt{q_{100}}$, the factorization above gives $S(r,\theta)\leq0$.  The
checker proves $\partial_rN(r,\theta)<-0.585$ throughout
$\sqrt{q_{100}}\leq r\leq\sqrt{0.9}$ by covering this rectangle with $1544$
directed rational boxes.  Hence $S(r,\theta)<0$ for every
$r>\sqrt{q_{100}}$ in this interval.  Its coefficients remain nonnegative
weights on finite cycle inequalities, so every
$q_{100}<q\leq0.9$ is infeasible. Lemma~\ref{lem:closed-rate-problem}
already gives $q_\star(10)\leq0.9$. Thus
\[
 \rho_{\rm fix}(100)=\rho_{\rm hor}(100)=q_\star(10)=q_{100}.
\]

The exact trajectory \eqref{eq:k100-tail} occupies four real dimensions and does not by itself enforce $x_{-1}=x_0$.
The construction in Lemma~\ref{lem:initialization-splice} scales this trajectory and adds one orthogonal scalar coordinate to $x_t$, equal to zero for $t\geq2$.
It therefore produces one function in
$\mathcal F_{1,100}(\mathbf R^5)$ with the standard initialization and asymptotic
factor $q_{100}$. Equation~\eqref{eq:k100-exact-decay} describes the
four-dimensional sequence in \eqref{eq:k100-tail}, not the five-dimensional
trajectory with $x_{-1}=x_0$.
Figure~\ref{fig:k100-multimode} shows an orthogonal
three-dimensional projection of the genuine four-dimensional tail.

name: Identification of the exact rate

label: eq:radical-polynomial-bridge
title: Proof
body_md:
\emph{Interpolation inequalities and the lower bound.}
We use the normalization of Appendix~\ref{app:uniform-upper-bound}, with
$p_s$ defined in \eqref{eq:inverse-transfer}. For
$z=\sqrt q\,e^{i\theta}$, $s=s_\dagger$, and $q>q_{\mathrm{quad}}(s)$, define
\[
 K_m(z)\doteq(1-\bar z)\frac{1-q^m}{1-q}+q^m-z^m,
 \qquad C_m^\sigma(q,\chi)\doteq\operatorname{Re}[p_s(z)K_m(z)].
\]
Here $C_m^\sigma$ is the sum of the interpolation terms around
$(0,1,\ldots,m,0)$ for $\sigma_t=z^t$, $r_t=p_s(z)z^t$. Unlike
$C_m^\pm$ in Appendix~\ref{app:kappa-ten}, it is a whole-cycle cost, not
the right-hand side of an individual comparison. These cycle costs are
rational functions of $(q,\chi)$, and
\[
 \mathcal C_{(0,1,\ldots,m,0)}^s(z)
   =(s^2-1)|z-\alpha_s|^4 C_m^\sigma(q,\chi).
\]
Since $s=s_\dagger$ is now fixed, $\alpha_s=\alpha_\dagger$ and
$|z-\alpha_\dagger|^2=q-\alpha_\dagger\chi+\alpha_\dagger^2$.
Combining this identity with \eqref{eq:radical-cycle-normalization} gives
the explicit relation to the polynomials:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:radical-polynomial-bridge}
 C_m^\sigma(q,\chi)=
 \frac{1+q-\chi}
 {2(s_\dagger^2-1)(q-\alpha_\dagger\chi+\alpha_\dagger^2)^2}
 P_m(\alpha_\dagger,q,\chi).
\end{equation}
The common factor is independent of $m$ and strictly positive for
$q_{\mathrm{quad}}(s_\dagger)<q<1$ and $|\chi|\leq2\sqrt q$.
In particular, the two
active polynomial equations are exactly $C_5^\sigma=C_6^\sigma=0$.

The isolated pair $(q_\dagger,\chi_\dagger)$ gives the complex multiplier
$z_\dagger\doteq\chi_\dagger/2+i\sqrt{q_\dagger-\chi_\dagger^2/4}$ for the contracting
and rotating component. Choose the value at index zero of the convex
interpolation function $\varphi$ from \eqref{eq:phi} to be
\[
 v\doteq\frac{\operatorname{Re}[p_s(z_\dagger)(1-\bar z_\dagger)]}
         {1-q_\dagger}.
\]
With $\varphi_t\doteq q_\dagger^t v$, the interpolation inequalities for
$(0,m)$ and $(m,0)$ from \eqref{eq:star-feasible}, expressed in this
normalization, are equivalent to
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:mixed-radical-all-lags}
 0\leq C_m^\sigma(q_\dagger,\chi_\dagger)
 \leq\operatorname{Re}p_s(z_\dagger)|1-z_\dagger^m|^2,
 \qquad m\geq1.
\end{equation}
The lower equalities at $m=5,6$ and the upper equality at $m=1$ follow
algebraically. They correspond to the active comparisons $(5,0)$, $(6,0)$,
and $(0,1)$, respectively. The upper inequalities at $m=5,6$ are strict
because $\operatorname{Re}p_s(z_\dagger)>0$ and $|z_\dagger|<1$.
Outward-rounded interval arithmetic verifies the positive real part and all
remaining inequalities for $m=1,\ldots,30$. Here $m$ is the difference
between the two iteration indices, not a bound on the iteration count. With
$K_\infty\doteq(1-\bar z)/(1-q)$ and
$C_\infty^\sigma\doteq\operatorname{Re}(p_s(z)K_\infty)$, the identity
\[
 C_m^\sigma=C_\infty^\sigma
       +q^m\operatorname{Re}[p_s(z)(1-K_\infty)]
       -\operatorname{Re}(p_s(z)z^m)
\]
gives geometric bounds for every $m\geq31$. The interval calculation shows
that both limiting margins are strictly larger than the corresponding
bounds on the remaining terms. Thus both inequalities hold for every
$m\geq1$. The positive rescaling in \eqref{eq:normalization-change} gives
an angular pair satisfying \eqref{eq:star-feasible} at $q=q_\dagger$.
Hence $q_\dagger\in\mathcal Q(s_\dagger)$, establishing the lower bound.

\emph{Ruling out larger asymptotic factors.}
For the upper bound, we need a positive weighted sum of cycle costs that is
strictly negative at every allowed angle when $q$ is just above $q_\dagger$.
We construct this function from the two active costs $C_5^\sigma$ and
$C_6^\sigma$. Both vanish at the candidate; we choose their weight so that
the derivative of the combination with respect to $\chi$ vanishes there
too. We therefore take the weight
\[
 \lambda_\dagger\doteq
 \frac{\partial_\chi C_6^\sigma(q_\dagger,\chi_\dagger)}
      {\partial_\chi C_6^\sigma(q_\dagger,\chi_\dagger)
        -\partial_\chi C_5^\sigma(q_\dagger,\chi_\dagger)}
 =0.4156030236805012584\ldots\in(0,1)
\]
and define the weighted sum, which in this case is a convex combination
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:radical-dual-combination}
 \Phi_\dagger(q,\chi)\doteq\lambda_\dagger C_5^\sigma(q,\chi)
 +(1-\lambda_\dagger)C_6^\sigma(q,\chi).
\end{equation}
Here $\lambda_\dagger$ and $1-\lambda_\dagger$ weight the two cycles, not two angles; the construction uses one rotating component.
By \eqref{eq:radical-polynomial-bridge}, this is equivalently
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:radical-polynomial-combination}
 \Phi_\dagger(q,\chi)=
 \frac{(1+q-\chi)\bigl[\lambda_\dagger P_5(\alpha_\dagger,q,\chi)
 +(1-\lambda_\dagger)P_6(\alpha_\dagger,q,\chi)\bigr]}
 {2(s_\dagger^2-1)(q-\alpha_\dagger\chi+\alpha_\dagger^2)^2}.
\end{equation}
Thus $\Phi_\dagger$ is an auxiliary rational function built from the two defining
polynomials, with the same sign as their weighted combination on the
allowed interval, which we use for the upper bound.
The elimination below uses the equations $P_5=P_6=0$ which only involve rational coefficients; note, we do not require the weight $\lambda_\dagger$ to be rational.
We keep $\lambda_\dagger$ fixed as $q$ varies. The algebraic definitions give
$\Phi_\dagger=\partial_\chi\Phi_\dagger=0$ at $(q_\dagger,\chi_\dagger)$.
Outward-rounded interval arithmetic establishes $\partial_{\chi\chi}\Phi_\dagger<-100$
on a neighborhood of $\chi_\dagger$ at $q=q_\dagger$, and
$\partial_q\Phi_\dagger(q_\dagger,\chi_\dagger)<-300$. The same method establishes a
strict negative bound away from $\chi_\dagger$ using finitely many intervals
with rational endpoints in $[-161/500,161/500]$, where
$2\sqrt{q_\dagger}<161/500$. An exact rational check confirms that these
intervals and the neighborhood used for the concavity bound together cover
the entire interval; no part of the allowed frequency interval is omitted.
Thus $\chi_\dagger$ is a zero-valued maximum of $\chi\mapsto\Phi_\dagger(q_\dagger,\chi)$.
This is the contact with the horizontal axis; the maximum, rather than a
minimum, reflects the sign of the cycle costs used here.

Local strict concavity and the negative partial derivative with respect to
$q$, together with the strict negative bound away from $\chi_\dagger$ on a
compact interval, make this same weighted sum strictly negative for every
allowed rotation angle when $q>q_\dagger$ is sufficiently close to
$q_\dagger$. Its coefficients are positive weights on finite cycle
inequalities. The positive normalization factor transfers it to the costs
of Lemma~\ref{lem:strict-alternative}.
Proposition~\ref{prop:strict-separator-rate} therefore gives
$\rho_{\mathrm{hor}}(\kappa_\dagger)\leq q$ for all such $q$. Letting
$q\downarrow q_\dagger$ and using Theorem~\ref{thm:main} gives
$q_\star(s_\dagger)\leq q_\dagger$. Feasibility supplies the reverse
inequality. This factor is also attained by a trajectory in $\mathbf R^2$ with
$x_{-1}=x_0$, using a separate choice of the initial point and first gradient
rather than the additional coordinate of Lemma~\ref{lem:initialization-splice}.

label: prop:rate-not-radical
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: A rate not expressible by radicals

title: Proof
body_md:
\emph{Eliminating the angle.}
The preceding example is determined by two active cycle constraints,
$P_5(\alpha_\dagger,q,\chi)=P_6(\alpha_\dagger,q,\chi)=0$.
Here $z=\sqrt q\,e^{i\theta}$, with $\theta\in[0,\pi]$, specifies the
contracting and rotating component: $q=|z|^2$ is its squared contraction
factor and $\chi=z+\bar z=2\sqrt q\cos\theta$ encodes its rotation angle.
The needed specialization of \eqref{eq:radical-cycle-polynomial} is
\[
\begin{aligned}
 T_0&=2,\qquad T_1=\chi,\qquad T_{j+1}=\chi T_j-qT_{j-1},\\
 H_m&=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}q^j,\\
 D_\dagger&\doteq2q^2-2\alpha_\dagger q\chi+\alpha_\dagger^2(\chi^2-2q),\\
 E_\dagger&\doteq(q^2+\alpha_\dagger^2q)\chi-4\alpha_\dagger q^2,
\end{aligned}
\]
and, for $m=5,6$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 P_m(\alpha_\dagger,q,\chi)=\frac1{\chi-1-q}\Bigl[&
 (D_\dagger-E_\dagger)H_m+q^mD_\dagger\\
 &{}-q^2T_m+2\alpha_\dagger qT_{m+1}
       -\alpha_\dagger^2T_{m+2}\Bigr].
\end{aligned}
\]
As before, the numerator is divisible by $\chi-1-q$, so these are polynomials.
We eliminate $\chi$ from the two polynomial equations by taking their
\emph{resultant}. This is a polynomial in $q$ alone that vanishes whenever
the equations have a common $\chi$ solution. Thus it gives a necessary
condition on $q$, algebraically projecting out $\chi$. It may also vanish
at values that do not correspond to an admissible trajectory, so we must
identify the relevant factor. Exact elimination gives, up to a nonzero
rational scalar,
\[
 \operatorname{Res}_\chi(P_5,P_6)
  =q^7(q+1)^2(q-\alpha_\dagger^2)^3
       (q^2-q+1)^2(q^2+q+1)^3F(q),
\]
where $P_m$ here denotes $P_m(\alpha_\dagger,q,\chi)$.
None of the factors preceding $F$ vanishes in $I$, so the common solution
from the preceding lemma satisfies $F(q_\dagger)=0$.
Sturm's rule, which counts real roots in a rational interval using exact
polynomial arithmetic, gives one root in $I$ and one in the smaller
$q$ interval isolating the common solution. The smaller interval lies in $I$.
This identifies the specified root of $F$ with $q_\star(s_\dagger)$.

\emph{Reading the modular factorizations.}
A polynomial is \emph{irreducible over $\mathbb Q$} if it cannot be factored
into two positive-degree polynomials with rational coefficients.
Rather than factor $F$ over $\mathbb Q$ directly, we reduce its integer
coefficients modulo a prime $p$ and factor using arithmetic modulo $p$.
Exact computation gives
\[
 \begin{array}{c|l}
 p&\text{degrees of the irreducible factors of }F\bmod p\\ \hline
 13&1,19\\
 107&1,1,2,3,13\\
 223&20
 \end{array}.
\]
The leading coefficients modulo these primes are $9$, $102$, and $124$,
respectively, so the degree does not drop. Each reduction is
\emph{squarefree}, meaning that no irreducible factor is repeated.

The \emph{Galois group} $\mathfrak{G}$ consists of the permutations of the complex roots
that preserve their algebraic relations over $\mathbb Q$.
Dedekind's theorem turns each row of the table into information about such
permutations: $\mathfrak{G}$ contains a permutation whose cycle lengths are precisely
the listed factor degrees~\citep[Theorem~4.28]{milne2022fields}.\footnote{The
cited theorem is stated for monic integer polynomials. With $a\doteq a_{20}$,
apply it to $a^{19}F(u/a)$, which is monic with integer coefficients and has
the same splitting field as $F$. At the three primes, $a$ is invertible,
so the change of variable and the scalar factor preserve factor degrees
and squarefreeness.}
Here cycles refer to permutations of polynomial roots, not to the
iteration-index comparisons used to construct $F$. A cycle of length $k$
sends each of $k$ roots to the next and the last back to the first, fixing
all other roots. The three rows give the following argument.
\begin{enumerate}
\item \emph{Irreducibility and transitivity.}
Modulo $223$, there is just one irreducible factor, of degree $20$.
Because the integer coefficients of $F$ have no common factor greater than
one and its leading coefficient is nonzero modulo $223$, this proves
irreducibility over $\mathbb Q$.
Consequently $\mathfrak{G}$ is \emph{transitive}: any root can be sent to any other
root by some permutation in $\mathfrak{G}$.
\item \emph{Moving pairs of roots.}
The row for $p=13$ supplies a $19$-cycle fixing the remaining root.
Its powers can send any of the other nineteen roots to any other while
keeping that root fixed. Transitivity gives the same property for any
choice of fixed root. Thus $\mathfrak{G}$ is \emph{$2$-transitive}: it can send any
ordered pair of distinct roots to any other such pair.
\item \emph{Swapping two roots.}
The row for $p=107$ supplies disjoint cycles of lengths $1,1,2,3,13$.
Applying that permutation $39=3\cdot13$ times makes the $3$- and $13$-cycles
return to their starting points, while the $2$-cycle still swaps its two
roots. The result is a \emph{transposition}, a permutation swapping just two
roots. By $2$-transitivity, relabelling this swap using elements of $\mathfrak{G}$
gives a swap of any chosen pair. Every permutation is a product of such
swaps, so $\mathfrak{G}=S_{20}$, the full symmetric group on the twenty roots.
\end{enumerate}

\emph{Excluding radicals.}
The needed consequence of the Galois criterion for solvability by radicals
is this: an irreducible polynomial over $\mathbb Q$ whose Galois group is
$S_n$, with $n\geq5$, has no root expressible by
radicals~\citep[Theorem~3.28 and its following discussion; proof in Theorem~5.34]{milne2022fields}.
Irreducibility matters here: a radical expression for one root would give
such expressions for all the other roots as well.
Since $F$ is irreducible and its group is $S_{20}$,
this excludes a radical expression for $q_\dagger$.
Evaluating an everywhere-defined radical formula with rational coefficients
at the rational input $s_\dagger$ would contradict this conclusion, proving
Remark~\ref{rem:no-radical-formula}. This does not preclude specifying the
rate as the unique root of a polynomial in an explicitly given interval,
as we have done here.

label: prop:radical-base-extensions
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:radical-base-extensions}
The factor $q_\dagger$ is not expressible by radicals over $\mathbb Q(\tau)$
for any number $\tau$ transcendental over $\mathbb Q$, nor over any finite
extension $E/\mathbb Q$ with $[E:\mathbb Q]<20$. Adjoining the answer itself
attains the bound: $\mathbb Q(q_\dagger)$ has degree $20$.
head: environment
name: Extensions at the certified parameter

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $L$ be the splitting field of $F$, so $\operatorname{Gal}(L/\mathbb Q)=S_{20}$.
A transcendental $\tau$ remains transcendental over $L$. Clearing denominators
and comparing coefficients of powers of $\tau$ shows that a basis of $L$ over $\mathbb Q$
stays linearly independent over $\mathbb Q(\tau)$; likewise for
$\mathbb Q(q_\dagger)$. Thus adjoining $\tau$ preserves the irreducibility
and group $S_{20}$ of $F$, excluding radical expressions for its roots.

For a finite extension $E$, the splitting group over $E$ identifies with
$\mathfrak{G}_E=\operatorname{Gal}(L/(L\cap E))$, a subgroup of $S_{20}$ of index
$d=[L\cap E:\mathbb Q]<20$. Acting on the cosets maps $S_{20}$ to $S_d$.
Since $20!/2>d!$, the simple alternating group $A_{20}$ of even permutations
cannot inject into $S_d$. Its action is therefore trivial, so $\mathfrak{G}_E$
contains $A_{20}$. This makes $\mathfrak{G}_E$ transitive and nonsolvable: $F$ stays
irreducible over $E$, and the radical criterion again applies.

label: prop:geometric-radical-obstruction
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:geometric-radical-obstruction}
There is an open interval $J\subset(1,\infty)$ containing $s_\dagger$ on
which $q_\star(s)$ is a real-analytic root of $H(1-1/s,q)$.
The splitting-field Galois group of $H$ over $\mathbb C(\alpha)$ is $S_{20}$.
Consequently no formula built from rational functions of $s$ with arbitrary
fixed complex coefficients and finitely many radicals agrees with $q_\star(s)$
on any nonempty open subinterval of $J$.
head: environment
name: No local radical formula with arbitrary fixed constants

title: Proof
body_md:
\emph{Persistence of the optimal branch.}
At the isolated common zero, outward-rounded evaluation gives
\[
 4.5\cdot10^{-8}
 <\det\frac{\partial(P_5,P_6)}{\partial(q,\chi)}
       (\alpha_\dagger,q_\dagger,\chi_\dagger)
 <4.6\cdot10^{-8}.
\]
The analytic implicit-function theorem continues $(q,\chi)$ locally in $s$,
preserving $q>\alpha_s^2$ and $\chi^2<4q$. The three active comparisons
remain equalities. All other finite inequalities in
Lemma~\ref{lem:mixed-radical-rate} have strict margins; its geometric tail
bounds remain uniform on a small compact neighborhood with $q<1$.
Thus interpolation feasibility persists. The dual weight remains in $(0,1)$;
strict concavity near contact, the negative test-$q$ derivative, and
uniform negativity away from contact also persist.
For each continued pair, hold its dual weight fixed as the test $q$ varies.
The same lower and strict-separator upper arguments identify the continued
factor with $q_\star(s)$. Shrink $J$ to exclude the other resultant factors.

\emph{Galois group over $\mathbb Q(\alpha)$.}
At $\alpha_\dagger$, the roots are distinct and their group is $S_{20}$.
Each root lifts uniquely to a formal power-series root in
$\alpha-\alpha_\dagger$, with coefficients in the splitting field $L$ of $F$.
Acting coefficientwise, $\operatorname{Gal}(L/\mathbb Q)$ permutes these
lifts faithfully because their constant terms are distinct. Thus the group
over $\mathbb Q(\alpha)$ contains, and hence equals, $S_{20}$.

\emph{Allowing arbitrary complex constants.}
The discriminant
$\mathcal{D}(\alpha)\doteq\operatorname{Disc}_qH(\alpha,q)\in\mathbb Z[\alpha]$
detects collisions of roots in $q$. Exact computation gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:generic-radical-branch-certificate}
 \mathcal{D}(8)\equiv0,\qquad \mathcal{D}'(8)\equiv25\pmod{29}.
\end{equation}
These congruences imply that $\mathcal{D}$ has a simple complex zero: if every
characteristic-zero irreducible factor were repeated, reduction modulo $29$
could not produce a simple root. Since the leading $q$ coefficient is the
nonzero constant $16$, a simple discriminant zero is a simple collision of
two roots; continuation around it exchanges those roots and fixes the others.
This transposition lies in the subgroup fixing the algebraic constant field,
called the geometric group. It is normal in $S_{20}$, so contains all
conjugate transpositions and equals $S_{20}$.
Extending the algebraically closed constants from
$\overline{\mathbb Q}$ to $\mathbb C$ preserves this group.

Hence $H$ is irreducible over $\mathbb C(\alpha)$ with nonsolvable group.
A radical expression agreeing with a root on an open interval would give a
radical algebraic branch over that field, contradicting the radical
criterion. The rational change $\alpha=1-1/s$ proves the claim.

title: Remark
body_md:
The contact coordinate and the rate generate the same degree-$20$ field:
$\mathbb Q(\chi_\dagger)=\mathbb Q(q_\dagger)$.
Exact elimination of the specialized $P_5,P_6$ gives rational-coefficient
relations $U(q)\chi+V(q)=0$ and $\widetilde U(\chi)q+\widetilde V(\chi)=0$.
Exact gcd checks exclude zeros of both leading coefficients at the isolated
pair, so each coordinate is recovered rationally from the other.
These obstructions do not exclude isolated-root descriptions or other
nonradical notions of closed form.
